foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Which organelle is the primary site of ATP synthesis via oxidative phosphorylation?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Mitochondria house the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The phospholipid bilayer of the plasma membrane is best described by which model?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Singer & Nicolson's fluid mosaic model describes proteins floating in a fluid lipid bilayer.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Which organelle is responsible for post-translational modification and packaging of proteins for secretion?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: The Golgi modifies, sorts, and packages proteins into vesicles.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Ribosomal RNA is synthesized in which structure?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: The nucleolus is the site of rRNA transcription and ribosome subunit assembly.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Which organelle contains hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases for digesting cellular debris and pathogens.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is most prominent in cells that:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is rich in enzymes for lipid/steroid synthesis and detoxification.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The passage of water across a cell membrane through specific channel proteins is called:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Aquaporins are water channels that speed water movement down its gradient.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Which transport process requires ATP and moves a substance against its concentration gradient?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Active transport uses ATP to move solutes against their gradient.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The Na+/K+-ATPase pump moves:
o: Equal Na+ and K+ in both directions
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: The pump extrudes 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+ per ATP hydrolyzed.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Which phase of the cell cycle involves DNA replication?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: DNA is replicated during S (synthesis) phase.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Sister chromatids separate during which phase of mitosis?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Anaphase is defined by sister chromatid separation to opposite poles.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs during:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Crossing over occurs at the pachytene stage of prophase I in meiosis.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The end product of meiosis in spermatogenesis is:
o: One ovum and three polar bodies
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Spermatogenesis produces four haploid spermatids from one spermatogonium.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: DNA replication is described as semiconservative because:
o: Only one daughter molecule retains parental DNA
Each daughter molecule has one parental and one new strand
DNA is degraded and resynthesized entirely
Each daughter molecule has two new strands
RNA primers persist in the final molecule
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Each new duplex retains one original template strand plus one newly synthesized strand.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The enzyme responsible for unwinding the DNA double helix at the replication fork is:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Helicase unwinds the parental duplex ahead of the replication fork.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Okazaki fragments are formed on the:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Which RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA in eukaryotic cells?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: RNA Pol II synthesizes pre-mRNA (and most snRNAs).

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The process of removing introns and joining exons in pre-mRNA is called:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Splicing removes non-coding introns and ligates exons together.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: A codon consists of how many nucleotides?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Each codon is a triplet of nucleotides specifying one amino acid (or stop).

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The site of protein synthesis (translation) is the:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Ribosomes (free or on rough ER) translate mRNA into polypeptide chains.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: A point mutation that changes a codon to a stop codon is called a:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: A nonsense mutation prematurely terminates translation.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Insertion or deletion of a number of bases not divisible by three causes a:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Non-triplet indels shift the reading frame downstream of the mutation.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: According to Mendel's law of segregation:
o: Two alleles for a trait separate during gamete formation
Dominant alleles always mask recessive ones completely in all cases
Genes for different traits assort independently
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Each gamete receives only one of the two alleles present in the parent.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: A cross between two heterozygous individuals (Aa x Aa) for a completely dominant trait yields a phenotypic ratio of:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: A monohybrid Aa x Aa cross gives a classic 3:1 dominant:recessive phenotypic ratio.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Down syndrome most commonly results from:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Meiotic nondisjunction producing trisomy 21 accounts for most cases.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Turner syndrome is characterized by the karyotype:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Turner syndrome results from a single X chromosome (45,X).

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Klinefelter syndrome karyotype is typically:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Klinefelter syndrome is classically 47,XXY.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that apoptosis:
o: Always affects groups of contiguous cells
Is a programmed, energy-dependent cell death without inflammation
Is triggered only by external trauma
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Apoptosis is a regulated, ATP-dependent process that avoids spilling cell contents and inflammation.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The mitochondrial genome is inherited:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Mitochondria (and their DNA) are passed almost exclusively from the mother via the ovum.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Barr bodies represent:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: A Barr body is a condensed, transcriptionally inactive X chromosome (Lyonization).

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Which cytoskeletal filament is composed of tubulin and forms the mitotic spindle?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Microtubules, built from tubulin dimers, form the spindle apparatus.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Centrioles are primarily composed of:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Centrioles are cylindrical microtubule structures organizing the spindle poles.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The primary function of peroxisomes is:
o: Beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids and H2O2 detoxification
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Peroxisomes break down very-long-chain fatty acids and detoxify hydrogen peroxide via catalase.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Chromatin exists in a highly condensed, transcriptionally inactive form called:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Heterochromatin is densely packed and largely transcriptionally silent.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: A nucleosome core particle consists of DNA wrapped around:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: DNA wraps around a histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4).

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: Telomerase functions to:
o: Add repetitive sequences to chromosome ends, preventing shortening
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Telomerase extends telomeric repeats, counteracting end-replication shortening.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: An autosomal recessive disorder is expressed phenotypically when:
o: The mutation is in mitochondrial DNA
Two copies of the mutant allele are inherited (homozygous)
One copy of the mutant allele is inherited
The gene is located on the X chromosome
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Recessive traits require two mutant alleles (homozygosity) for expression.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: X-linked recessive disorders are:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes, so one mutant allele causes expression.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: A pedigree showing affected individuals in every generation with no skipping is most consistent with:
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: Autosomal dominant traits typically appear in every generation without skipping.

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.s: The Golgi apparatus modifies proteins by adding which type of group in glycosylation?
foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.e: The Golgi adds and trims oligosaccharide chains onto proteins passing through it.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The universal energy currency of the cell is:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: ATP's high-energy phosphate bonds power most cellular work.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Glycolysis takes place in the:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Glycolysis is a cytosolic pathway, independent of mitochondria.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The net ATP yield from glycolysis (glucose to 2 pyruvate) is:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: 4 ATP are produced and 2 consumed, for a net of 2 ATP.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis is:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: PFK-1 catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The citric acid (Krebs) cycle occurs in the:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: TCA cycle enzymes reside in the mitochondrial matrix.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Which molecule is regenerated to accept a new acetyl group at the start of each turn of the TCA cycle?
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Oxaloacetate condenses with acetyl-CoA to form citrate, restarting the cycle.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The electron transport chain is located in the:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: ETC complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain is:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Oxygen accepts electrons at Complex IV, forming water.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: ATP synthase generates ATP using the energy of:
o: A proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Chemiosmotic proton flow through ATP synthase drives ATP synthesis.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Complete oxidation of one glucose molecule yields approximately how many ATP (theoretical maximum, textbook value)?
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Modern textbook estimates of net ATP from full glucose oxidation are ~30-32.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: An enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction by:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Enzymes speed reactions by stabilizing the transition state, not by altering equilibrium.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Km represents:
o: Substrate concentration at half of Vmax
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Km is the substrate concentration at which velocity equals half Vmax.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: A low Km value indicates:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: A low Km means half-maximal velocity is reached at low substrate, i.e. high affinity.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: A competitive inhibitor:
o: Binds the active site and can be overcome by increasing substrate
Has no structural resemblance to substrate
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and compete for the active site; excess substrate outcompetes them.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: A noncompetitive inhibitor typically:
o: Has no effect on enzyme activity
Competes with substrate for the active site
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme, lowering Vmax while Km is unchanged.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Most water-soluble vitamins function biochemically as:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: B-vitamins largely serve as precursors to metabolic coenzymes.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a cofactor for:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Niacin (vitamin B3) is incorporated into the coenzymes:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Niacin is the precursor of NAD+/NADP+, central redox coenzymes.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is a precursor of:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Riboflavin forms the redox coenzymes FAD and FMN.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is a component of:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Pantothenic acid is incorporated into coenzyme A, central to acyl-group transfer.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: An exergonic reaction is one that:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Exergonic reactions have negative delta-G and release free energy, proceeding spontaneously.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Enzymes are classified into six major classes by the IUBMB. Which class catalyzes transfer of a functional group between molecules?
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Transferases move functional groups (e.g., phosphate, amino) between molecules.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Enzymes that catalyze hydrolysis reactions belong to the class:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Hydrolases cleave bonds using water, e.g. proteases, lipases.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The pH of arterial blood is normally maintained at approximately:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Normal arterial pH is tightly regulated between 7.35 and 7.45.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The most important extracellular buffer system in blood is the:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: The bicarbonate/carbonic acid system is the principal extracellular buffer.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Allosteric enzymes typically show which kinetic pattern instead of classic Michaelis-Menten hyperbolic kinetics?
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Cooperative binding in allosteric enzymes produces a sigmoidal velocity curve.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids occurs primarily in the:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Fatty acyl-CoA is broken down two carbons at a time in the mitochondrial matrix.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The gluconeogenesis pathway primarily occurs in the:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: The liver (and to a lesser extent renal cortex) is the main site of gluconeogenesis.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Ketone bodies are produced mainly during:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Ketogenesis rises when fatty acid oxidation predominates during fasting/starvation.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The pentose phosphate pathway primarily generates:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: The PPP produces NADPH for biosynthesis/antioxidant defense and ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis) is stimulated primarily by:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Insulin promotes glycogen synthase activity, favoring glycogen storage in the fed state.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) in the liver is stimulated mainly by:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Glucagon and epinephrine activate glycogen phosphorylase, releasing glucose.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The cofactor required by pyruvate carboxylase (first step of gluconeogenesis) is:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent carboxylase.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Lactate produced in exercising muscle is converted back to glucose in the liver via the:
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: The Cori cycle shuttles lactate from muscle to liver for gluconeogenesis.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: An enzyme's turnover number (kcat) reflects:
o: The pH optimum of the enzyme
The number of substrate molecules converted to product per enzyme molecule per unit time at saturation
The number of active sites only
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: kcat is the catalytic constant describing maximal substrate turnover per active site.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Zymogens (proenzymes) are:
o: Inactive precursors that require proteolytic cleavage for activation
Always found only in the cytosol
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Zymogens like pepsinogen and trypsinogen need cleavage to become catalytically active.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Feedback inhibition in a metabolic pathway typically occurs when:
o: The initial substrate activates the first enzyme
The pathway's end product inhibits an early, often rate-limiting, enzyme
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: End-product feedback inhibition regulates flux by acting on an early committed step.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) acts as a cofactor in which biochemical process relevant to connective tissue?
o: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen synthesis
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: Vitamin C is required for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase activity in collagen maturation.

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.s: The Bohr effect describes how:
o: pH has no effect on hemoglobin function
Hemoglobin releases CO2 instead of O2
Increased CO2 and H+ (lower pH) decrease hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, promoting O2 release to tissues
Oxygen affinity of hemoglobin increases with rising CO2/H+
foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.e: The Bohr effect facilitates oxygen unloading in metabolically active, acidic tissue.

foundation/general-histology.s: Simple squamous epithelium is characteristically found lining the:
foundation/general-histology.e: Thin simple squamous epithelium lines alveoli and vessels, suited to diffusion.

foundation/general-histology.s: Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium is typically found in the:
foundation/general-histology.e: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, protective against abrasion/water loss.

foundation/general-histology.s: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells is characteristic of the:
foundation/general-histology.e: This respiratory epithelium moves mucus via ciliary action.

foundation/general-histology.s: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) is found in the:
foundation/general-histology.e: Transitional epithelium stretches to accommodate variable urine volume.

foundation/general-histology.s: Simple columnar epithelium with microvilli lines the:
foundation/general-histology.e: Absorptive enterocytes with a brush border line the small intestine.

foundation/general-histology.s: Which connective tissue cell type is primarily responsible for synthesizing collagen and ground substance?
foundation/general-histology.e: Fibroblasts are the principal matrix-producing cells of connective tissue.

foundation/general-histology.s: Mast cells release which substance during an allergic response?
foundation/general-histology.e: Mast cell degranulation releases histamine and other mediators.

foundation/general-histology.s: Hyaline cartilage is found at the:
foundation/general-histology.e: Hyaline cartilage covers articular surfaces, providing a smooth, low-friction joint surface.

foundation/general-histology.s: Elastic cartilage is characteristically found in the:
o: Pinna of the ear and epiglottis
foundation/general-histology.e: Elastic fibers give the pinna and epiglottis flexibility with recoil.

foundation/general-histology.s: Fibrocartilage is typically found in the:
foundation/general-histology.e: Fibrocartilage's dense collagen bundles resist compressive and shear forces at these sites.

foundation/general-histology.s: Compact bone's structural unit is the:
foundation/general-histology.e: The osteon, with its central Haversian canal and concentric lamellae, is compact bone's unit.

foundation/general-histology.s: Osteoblasts are responsible for:
foundation/general-histology.e: Osteoblasts synthesize and mineralize new bone matrix.

foundation/general-histology.s: Osteoclasts are derived from:
foundation/general-histology.e: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells of hematopoietic (monocyte) origin that resorb bone.

foundation/general-histology.s: Skeletal muscle fibers are characteristically:
o: Multinucleated and striated, under voluntary control
foundation/general-histology.e: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated, striated, and voluntarily controlled.

foundation/general-histology.s: Cardiac muscle is distinguished histologically by the presence of:
foundation/general-histology.e: Intercalated discs mechanically and electrically couple cardiac myocytes.

foundation/general-histology.s: Smooth muscle cells are characterized by:
o: A single central nucleus and no striations
foundation/general-histology.e: Smooth muscle is non-striated, spindle-shaped, with one central nucleus, under involuntary control.

foundation/general-histology.s: The functional unit of the nervous tissue is the:
foundation/general-histology.e: The neuron is the basic signaling unit of the nervous system.

foundation/general-histology.s: Myelin in the peripheral nervous system is produced by:
foundation/general-histology.e: Schwann cells myelinate individual peripheral axon segments.

foundation/general-histology.s: In the central nervous system, myelin is produced by:
foundation/general-histology.e: One oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple CNS axon segments.

foundation/general-histology.s: Exocrine glands release their secretions:
o: Via ducts onto an epithelial surface
Into the extracellular matrix without ducts
foundation/general-histology.e: Exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface, unlike ductless endocrine glands.

foundation/general-histology.s: Endocrine glands are distinguished from exocrine glands by:
o: Secreting hormones directly into the blood, ductless
foundation/general-histology.e: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the bloodstream.

foundation/general-histology.s: A gland with a single unbranched duct and a coiled tubular secretory portion (e.g., sweat gland) is classified as:
foundation/general-histology.e: Sweat glands are classic simple coiled tubular exocrine glands.

foundation/general-histology.s: The basement membrane functionally:
o: Has no biological role, purely structural artifact
Anchors epithelium to underlying connective tissue and regulates molecule passage
Is found only in muscle tissue
foundation/general-histology.e: The basement membrane provides structural anchorage and a selective filtration barrier.

foundation/general-histology.s: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) primarily function to:
o: Provide mechanical strength via intermediate filaments only
Anchor cells to the basement membrane
Allow direct ion passage between cells
Prevent paracellular movement of molecules, maintaining barrier function
foundation/general-histology.e: Tight junctions seal the intercellular space, controlling paracellular transport.

foundation/general-histology.s: Desmosomes (macula adherens) primarily provide:
foundation/general-histology.e: Desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments between cells, resisting mechanical stress.

foundation/general-histology.s: Gap junctions allow:
o: Direct cytoplasmic and electrical communication between adjacent cells
foundation/general-histology.e: Connexons forming gap junctions permit ion and small molecule passage, enabling electrical coupling.

foundation/general-histology.s: Adipose tissue is classified histologically as a variant of:
foundation/general-histology.e: Adipocytes and their supporting matrix constitute a specialized connective tissue.

foundation/general-histology.s: White adipose tissue cells typically show:
o: A single large lipid droplet with a peripherally flattened nucleus
Multiple small lipid droplets and many mitochondria
foundation/general-histology.e: Unilocular white adipocytes store one large lipid droplet, pushing the nucleus to the periphery.

foundation/general-histology.s: Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining shows hematoxylin staining structures:
foundation/general-histology.e: Hematoxylin is a basic dye that stains acidic/basophilic structures like nuclei blue-purple.

foundation/general-histology.s: Reticular connective tissue, rich in type III collagen, forms the supporting framework of:
o: Lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow)
foundation/general-histology.e: Reticular fibers form the delicate stromal meshwork of lymphoid and hematopoietic organs.

foundation/general-histology.s: Merkel cells in the epidermis primarily function in:
foundation/general-histology.e: Merkel cells are slow-adapting touch receptors in the basal epidermis.

foundation/general-histology.s: Langerhans cells in the epidermis are primarily:
o: Antigen-presenting dendritic cells of the immune system
foundation/general-histology.e: Langerhans cells are epidermal dendritic antigen-presenting cells.

foundation/general-histology.s: Melanocytes are located in which layer of the epidermis?
foundation/general-histology.e: Melanocytes reside in the stratum basale, transferring melanin to keratinocytes.

foundation/general-histology.s: Sebaceous glands secrete by which mechanism?
foundation/general-histology.e: Sebaceous glands release sebum by holocrine secretion, with cell disintegration.

foundation/general-histology.s: Apocrine sweat glands, distinct from eccrine glands, are typically located in:
o: Axilla and groin, becoming active at puberty
foundation/general-histology.e: Apocrine glands are concentrated in axillary/anogenital skin and activate at puberty.

foundation/general-histology.s: Which type of cartilage lacks a perichondrium?
o: Hyaline cartilage at joint surfaces (articular) and fibrocartilage
foundation/general-histology.e: Articular hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage characteristically lack a perichondrium.

foundation/general-histology.s: Woven bone differs from lamellar bone in that woven bone:
o: Has randomly oriented collagen fibers and is seen in fetal bone/healing fractures
Is the mature, organized adult bone pattern
foundation/general-histology.e: Woven bone is immature, disorganized bone later remodeled into lamellar bone.

foundation/general-histology.s: The perimysium in skeletal muscle surrounds:
foundation/general-histology.e: Perimysium is the connective tissue sheath around fascicles of muscle fibers.

foundation/general-histology.s: The endomysium surrounds:
foundation/general-histology.e: Endomysium is the delicate connective tissue around each individual muscle fiber.

foundation/general-histology.s: Satellite cells in skeletal muscle function primarily in:
foundation/general-histology.e: Satellite cells are muscle stem cells activated for repair and regeneration.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Oogenesis is arrested at which stage until ovulation?
foundation/general-embryology.e: Primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I from fetal life until just before ovulation.

foundation/general-embryology.s: At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested at:
foundation/general-embryology.e: The secondary oocyte is released arrested at metaphase II, completing meiosis only upon fertilization.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Fertilization normally occurs in the:
foundation/general-embryology.e: The ampulla is the usual site where sperm meets the secondary oocyte.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The zona pellucida's acrosome reaction-triggering role belongs to which sperm structure?
foundation/general-embryology.e: The acrosome releases enzymes that allow sperm penetration of the zona pellucida.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Cleavage of the zygote refers to:
o: Growth in cell size without division
Rapid mitotic division without overall size increase
foundation/general-embryology.e: Cleavage divisions increase cell number while total embryo size stays roughly constant.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The morula is composed of approximately how many cells (blastomeres)?
foundation/general-embryology.e: By convention the morula stage is reached at roughly the 16-cell solid ball stage.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The blastocyst forms a fluid-filled cavity called the:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Fluid accumulation within the morula creates the blastocele, defining the blastocyst.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The inner cell mass of the blastocyst gives rise to the:
foundation/general-embryology.e: The inner cell mass (embryoblast) forms the embryo itself.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The trophoblast differentiates into which two layers?
foundation/general-embryology.e: The trophoblast splits into an inner cellular cytotrophoblast and outer syncytiotrophoblast.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Implantation of the blastocyst normally occurs approximately how many days after fertilization?
foundation/general-embryology.e: Implantation typically begins around day 6-7 post-fertilization.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Implantation most commonly occurs in the:
o: Posterior superior wall of the uterine body
foundation/general-embryology.e: The posterior-superior uterine wall is the most common normal implantation site.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Gastrulation results in the formation of:
o: Three primary germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm)
foundation/general-embryology.e: Gastrulation converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar embryo.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The primitive streak defines the:
o: Cranio-caudal axis and site of gastrulation
foundation/general-embryology.e: The primitive streak establishes the embryonic axis and is where cells ingress during gastrulation.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Notochordal signaling induces neural plate formation (primary neural induction).

foundation/general-embryology.s: Neurulation refers to the formation of the:
o: Neural tube from the neural plate
foundation/general-embryology.e: Neurulation is the folding and closure of the neural plate into the neural tube.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Failure of neural tube closure at the cranial end results in:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Cranial neuropore closure failure produces anencephaly.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Failure of neural tube closure at the caudal end results in:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Caudal neuropore closure failure produces spina bifida.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The epidermis of the skin and nervous system both derive from which germ layer?
foundation/general-embryology.e: Surface ectoderm forms epidermis; neuroectoderm forms the nervous system.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The gastrointestinal tract epithelium and lining of the respiratory tract derive mainly from:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Endoderm lines the primitive gut tube and its derivatives, including respiratory epithelium.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Skeletal muscle, bone, cartilage, and the cardiovascular system derive primarily from:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Mesoderm gives rise to the musculoskeletal and cardiovascular systems.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Neural crest cells contribute to which of the following structures?
o: Melanocytes, cranial ganglia, and adrenal medulla
foundation/general-embryology.e: Neural crest is a versatile ectodermal population giving rise to these and many other structures.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The placenta functions primarily through the:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Chorionic villi are the functional exchange units of the placenta.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The umbilical cord normally contains:
foundation/general-embryology.e: The normal cord has two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Monozygotic twins arising from splitting of the inner cell mass (after chorion forms, before amnion forms) result in:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Splitting at this stage shares one chorion but produces two amnions.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Dizygotic twins are always:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Two separately fertilized zygotes implant with their own chorion and amnion.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The most critical period of susceptibility to teratogens for major structural malformations is:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Organogenesis (weeks 3-8) is the period of greatest vulnerability to structural teratogenesis.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The yolk sac's early function includes:
o: Early hematopoiesis and origin of primordial germ cells
foundation/general-embryology.e: The yolk sac is an early site of blood cell formation and germ cell origin.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Amniotic fluid functions include:
o: Cushioning the embryo and allowing symmetric growth
Serving as the site of fertilization
foundation/general-embryology.e: Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus and permits symmetric musculoskeletal development.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The bilaminar embryonic disc consists of:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Before gastrulation the disc is two layers: epiblast and hypoblast.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Situs inversus results from an abnormality of:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Disrupted left-right patterning signals during gastrulation can mirror-image the visceral organs.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The primitive node (Hensen's node) is important because it:
o: Organizes axial structures and induces notochord formation
foundation/general-embryology.e: Hensen's node is the organizer directing notochordal and axial development.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Somites, which give rise to vertebrae, ribs, and skeletal muscle, differentiate from:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites, forming axial skeleton and muscle.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The intermediate mesoderm gives rise mainly to:
foundation/general-embryology.e: Intermediate mesoderm forms the kidneys, gonads, and genital ducts.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Lateral plate mesoderm splits into somatic and splanchnic layers, which together form the:
o: Intraembryonic coelom (body cavity) lining and associated structures
foundation/general-embryology.e: The split lateral plate lines the future body cavities and contributes to serous membranes.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The heart begins to beat around which week of gestation?
foundation/general-embryology.e: The primitive heart tube begins rhythmic contractions around day 22-23.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Which pharyngeal arch gives rise to the muscles of mastication and the mandible?
foundation/general-embryology.e: The first (mandibular) arch forms the mandible and muscles of mastication (CN V).

foundation/general-embryology.s: The second pharyngeal arch (Reichert's cartilage derivatives) contributes to:
o: Muscles of facial expression and the stapes
foundation/general-embryology.e: The second (hyoid) arch is supplied by CN VII and forms facial expression muscles and the stapes.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Cloacal membrane division by the urorectal septum separates it into:
o: The urogenital sinus (anteriorly) and anal canal (posteriorly)
foundation/general-embryology.e: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into urogenital and anorectal components.

foundation/general-embryology.s: Fetal circulation shunts oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein past the liver primarily via the:
foundation/general-embryology.e: The ductus venosus bypasses the hepatic sinusoids, directing oxygenated blood toward the heart.

foundation/general-embryology.s: The foramen ovale in fetal circulation allows blood to shunt from the:
o: Right atrium to left atrium, bypassing the lungs
foundation/general-embryology.e: The foramen ovale directs oxygenated blood from the right to left atrium, bypassing non-functional fetal lungs.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Primary prevention aims to:
o: Prevent disease occurrence before it develops (e.g., vaccination)
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Primary prevention acts before disease onset, e.g. immunization, health promotion.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Secondary prevention is best exemplified by:
o: Screening programs for early detection (e.g., Pap smear)
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Secondary prevention detects disease early, often subclinically, via screening.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Tertiary prevention focuses on:
o: Limiting disability and rehabilitation after disease has occurred
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Tertiary prevention reduces complications/disability once disease is established.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Incidence measures:
o: The proportion of a population that has died
The number of people at risk only
The number of new cases occurring in a population over a specified period
The total number of existing cases at a point in time
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Incidence captures new cases arising during a defined time period.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Prevalence measures:
o: The total number of existing cases (new + old) at a given time
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Prevalence is a snapshot of all current cases, new and pre-existing.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A cohort study design:
o: Starts with disease status and looks back at exposure
Studies only prevalence at one point in time
Follows exposed and unexposed groups forward in time to observe outcomes
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Cohort studies follow groups defined by exposure status forward to observe outcomes.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A case-control study:
o: Follows subjects forward from exposure to outcome
Is the strongest design for establishing causation
Selects subjects based on outcome (cases vs controls) and looks backward at exposure
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Case-control studies work backward from outcome to prior exposure.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) minimizes bias primarily through:
o: Random allocation of participants to intervention/control groups
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Randomization balances known and unknown confounders between groups.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome:
o: Simultaneously, at a single point in time
At different points in time, sequentially
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Cross-sectional studies capture a single snapshot of exposure and outcome together.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: The mean of a data set is:
o: The middle value when data is ordered
The difference between the largest and smallest values
The sum of all values divided by the number of values
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: The arithmetic mean is the sum of observations divided by their count.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: The median of a data set is:
o: The middle value when data is arranged in order
The square root of the variance
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: The median is the central value of an ordered data set, less affected by outliers than the mean.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: The mode of a data set refers to:
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: The mode is simply the most common observation in a data set.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Standard deviation is a measure of:
o: The spread/dispersion of data around the mean
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Standard deviation quantifies how much individual values deviate from the mean.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: In a normal (Gaussian) distribution, approximately what percentage of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: By the empirical rule, ~68% of values fall within ±1 SD of the mean.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Simple random sampling ensures:
o: Every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
Every individual is deliberately excluded if inconvenient
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Simple random sampling gives each population member an equal selection probability.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Stratified sampling involves:
o: Dividing the population into subgroups (strata) and sampling from each
Selecting only the first available individuals
Selecting a sample purely by convenience
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Stratified sampling ensures representation from each defined subgroup.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Sensitivity of a screening test refers to:
o: The proportion of true negatives correctly identified
The proportion of healthy people who test negative
The proportion of people with disease who test positive (true positive rate)
The predictive value of a positive test
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Sensitivity is the test's ability to correctly identify those with disease.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Specificity of a screening test refers to:
o: The proportion of diseased people testing positive
The proportion of people without disease who test negative (true negative rate)
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Specificity is the test's ability to correctly identify those without disease.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Positive predictive value (PPV) is defined as:
o: The probability that a person with a negative test truly does not have the disease
The probability that a person with a positive test truly has the disease
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: PPV tells you, given a positive result, how likely disease is truly present; it varies with prevalence.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A confounding variable is one that:
o: Is independently associated with both exposure and outcome, distorting the true association
Is on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome
Is only relevant in cross-sectional studies
Has no relationship to exposure or outcome
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: A true confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome without being an intermediate step.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Selection bias occurs when:
o: The sample size is too large
The study sample is not representative of the target population due to how subjects were chosen
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Selection bias arises from non-representative recruitment or enrollment of subjects.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Recall bias is most likely to affect which study design?
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Case-control studies rely on retrospective recall, which differs systematically between cases and controls.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) schedule in most national programs recommends BCG vaccine be given:
o: At birth or as soon as possible after birth
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: BCG is typically given as a single dose at or soon after birth.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Infant mortality rate (IMR) is defined as:
o: Deaths of children under 5 years per 1000 live births
Deaths of infants per 1000 total population
Deaths of neonates per 1000 total births
Deaths of infants under 1 year of age per 1000 live births in a given year
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: IMR specifically counts deaths under age 1 per 1000 live births in a year.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is typically expressed as:
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: MMR is conventionally reported per 100,000 live births.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Herd immunity threshold depends primarily on:
o: The age of the population only
The basic reproduction number (R0) of the disease
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: The herd immunity threshold is mathematically derived from R0 (1 - 1/R0).

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Which of the following is a communicable disease control strategy targeting the reservoir?
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Isolating/treating infected persons directly reduces the human reservoir of infection.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A null hypothesis in biostatistics typically states that:
o: There is a significant difference/association between groups
There is no difference/association between groups being compared
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: The null hypothesis posits no true effect or difference, which testing tries to reject or fail to reject.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A p-value of less than 0.05 conventionally indicates:
o: The null hypothesis is definitely true
Statistically significant result at the 5% significance level, rejecting the null hypothesis
The result has no clinical significance
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: By convention, p<0.05 is taken as evidence against the null hypothesis at the 5% level.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Type I error in hypothesis testing refers to:
o: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive)
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative)
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: The demographic transition model describes changes in:
o: Birth and death rates as a country develops economically
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: The model tracks shifting birth/death rate patterns through stages of economic development.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals primarily by:
o: Reducing the overall circulation of the pathogen in the population
Eliminating the pathogen's reservoir entirely always
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: High population immunity limits transmission, indirectly protecting the unvaccinated.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: A case fatality rate is defined as:
o: Deaths from all causes per 1000 population
The proportion of people with a specific disease who die from it
Total deaths in a population per year
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Case fatality rate is deaths among diagnosed cases of a specific disease.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Crude birth rate is expressed as:
o: Live births per 100,000 women of reproductive age
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Crude birth rate is live births per 1000 total mid-year population in a year.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Relative risk (risk ratio) is calculated in which study design most directly?
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Cohort studies and RCTs directly measure incidence in exposed/unexposed groups, allowing relative risk calculation.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: An odds ratio approximates relative risk best when:
o: The study is a cohort study
The disease is rare in the population studied
There is no confounding regardless of prevalence
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: The rare disease assumption makes the odds ratio a good approximation of relative risk.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Bias that arises from measurement or classification error is termed:
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Information bias results from inaccurate measurement or misclassification of exposure/outcome.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Randomization in an RCT primarily protects against:
o: Confounding by balancing known and unknown variables between groups
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Randomization tends to evenly distribute confounders across study arms.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: Blinding (masking) in a clinical trial is used primarily to reduce:
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: Blinding reduces bias from expectations affecting outcome assessment or behavior.

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.s: The World Health Organization defines health as:
o: A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity
The mere absence of disease or infirmity
foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.e: WHO's definition explicitly extends health beyond the mere absence of disease.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: In adults, hematopoiesis normally occurs mainly in the:
o: Red bone marrow of axial skeleton and proximal long bones
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Adult hematopoiesis is confined mainly to red marrow of flat bones and proximal long bone epiphyses.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: During fetal life, the liver is the major site of hematopoiesis during which period?
o: Never; the liver is not a fetal hematopoietic site
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Hepatic hematopoiesis predominates through much of the second trimester before marrow takes over.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by the:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Renal peritubular cells sense hypoxia and secrete erythropoietin.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: The primary stimulus for erythropoietin secretion is:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Erythropoietin release is driven by hypoxia sensing in the kidney.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Mature red blood cells lack a nucleus and:
o: Both nucleus and mitochondria (rely on anaerobic glycolysis)
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Mature RBCs extrude their nucleus and lack mitochondria, depending on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: The average lifespan of a circulating red blood cell is approximately:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: RBCs survive roughly 120 days before removal by the reticuloendothelial system.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Aged red blood cells are primarily removed by macrophages in the:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Splenic and hepatic macrophages phagocytose senescent erythrocytes.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Hemoglobin is composed of:
o: Four heme groups and two globin chains
One globin chain with four heme groups
Four globin chains, each with one heme group
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Adult hemoglobin (HbA) is a tetramer of two alpha and two beta chains, each carrying one heme.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: The predominant hemoglobin in normal adults (HbA) has the chain composition:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: HbA (alpha2beta2) makes up the majority of adult hemoglobin.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) has the chain composition:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: HbF (alpha2gamma2) predominates in fetal life and has higher oxygen affinity than HbA.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Iron in the diet is absorbed most efficiently in which form?
o: Ferric (Fe3+) form found in plant sources
Ferrous (Fe2+) heme iron from animal sources
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Heme iron (Fe2+) from animal sources is absorbed more efficiently than non-heme iron.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Dietary iron absorption occurs mainly in the:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: The duodenum and upper jejunum are the principal sites of iron absorption.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Transferrin's main function is to:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Transferrin is the plasma protein that carries iron to tissues, particularly bone marrow.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Ferritin serves as the:
o: Structural protein of the RBC membrane
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Ferritin stores iron within cells, especially in liver, spleen, and marrow.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum requires binding to:
o: Intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Intrinsic factor-B12 complex is absorbed via specific receptors in the terminal ileum.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Deficiency of intrinsic factor leads to:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Lack of intrinsic factor impairs B12 absorption, causing pernicious anemia.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Folate deficiency and vitamin B12 deficiency both classically cause:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Both deficiencies impair DNA synthesis, producing large, immature megaloblastic red cells.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: The hematocrit is defined as:
o: The white cell count per microliter
The percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Hematocrit is the packed cell volume, the fraction of whole blood composed of RBCs.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is used to classify anemia as:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: MCV categorizes red cell size, guiding the differential diagnosis of anemia.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Reticulocytes are:
o: Immature red blood cells that still contain residual RNA
Damaged red blood cells destined for hemolysis
Mature red blood cells with full hemoglobin content and no organelles
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Reticulocytes are young RBCs with residual ribosomal RNA, indicating marrow output.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: A high reticulocyte count in an anemic patient suggests:
o: Appropriate marrow response, e.g. to hemolysis or blood loss
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Reticulocytosis indicates the marrow is actively compensating, as in hemolysis or hemorrhage.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in red blood cells functions to:
o: Decrease hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, facilitating O2 unloading to tissues
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin, shifting the curve right and promoting oxygen release.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: An increase in altitude (chronic hypoxia) leads to which compensatory change?
o: Increased plasma volume only, with no RBC change
Decreased erythropoietin and reduced RBC count
Increased erythropoietin and increased RBC mass (polycythemia)
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Chronic hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin, raising red cell mass to improve oxygen delivery.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: The RBC membrane protein spectrin functions mainly to:
o: Provide structural support and flexibility to the cell membrane cytoskeleton
Serve as a blood group antigen
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Spectrin forms a cytoskeletal network maintaining RBC shape and deformability.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Hereditary spherocytosis results from a defect in:
o: RBC membrane cytoskeletal proteins (e.g., spectrin, ankyrin)
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Membrane protein defects make red cells spherical and fragile, prone to splenic destruction.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Which laboratory index reflects the average hemoglobin content per red blood cell?
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: MCH is the average mass of hemoglobin per red blood cell.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Red cell distribution width (RDW) reflects:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: RDW quantifies the degree of variability in red blood cell volume.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Extramedullary hematopoiesis (outside bone marrow) in adults most commonly occurs in the:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: When marrow is insufficient, the liver and spleen can resume fetal-type hematopoiesis.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Which growth factor primarily stimulates megakaryocyte proliferation for platelet production?
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Thrombopoietin, mainly from the liver, drives megakaryocyte development.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Anemia of chronic disease is typically associated with:
o: Functional iron restriction due to elevated hepcidin, despite adequate body iron stores
Elevated serum iron and high transferrin saturation
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Inflammation raises hepcidin, trapping iron in stores and limiting its availability for erythropoiesis.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: The Hb-O2 dissociation curve shifts to the right (reduced affinity) with:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Higher temperature, 2,3-BPG, and acidity (as in active tissue) shift the curve right, favoring O2 unloading.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by:
o: Impaired heme synthesis leading to iron-laden mitochondria (ring sideroblasts) despite adequate iron
Normal iron utilization with defective globin synthesis
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Defective heme synthesis traps iron in mitochondria, producing ringed sideroblasts.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Thalassemia results from:
o: Abnormal hemoglobin structure due to a single amino acid substitution
Reduced or absent synthesis of one or more globin chains
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Thalassemias are quantitative defects in globin chain production (alpha or beta).

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Sickle cell disease results from a mutation causing:
o: Deletion of the entire beta-globin gene
Extra copies of the alpha-globin gene
Substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of beta-globin
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: A single glutamic acid-to-valine substitution produces HbS, which polymerizes under hypoxia.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Under conditions of hypoxia, HbS polymerization causes red cells to:
o: Sickle, becoming rigid and prone to vaso-occlusion
Shrink and lyse immediately in circulation always
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Polymerized HbS distorts the cell into a rigid sickle shape, promoting vaso-occlusion and hemolysis.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Which stain is classically used to identify reticulocytes under the microscope?
o: Supravital stains such as new methylene blue
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Supravital dyes precipitate residual RNA in reticulocytes, making them visible as a reticular network.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Normal hemoglobin concentration in adult males is approximately:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Normal adult male hemoglobin reference range is roughly 13.5-17.5 g/dL.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: Polycythemia vera is a disorder characterized by:
o: Excess destruction of red blood cells
Autonomous, excessive proliferation of red blood cells (often with a JAK2 mutation)
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder with clonal overproduction of red cells.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: The main site of physiological red cell destruction (extravascular hemolysis) is the:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Splenic macrophages are the principal site for removing aged or defective red cells.

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.s: An elevated unconjugated bilirubin with increased reticulocytes most suggests:
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.e: Hemolysis releases hemoglobin, raising unconjugated bilirubin, while the marrow compensates with reticulocytosis.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: The most abundant white blood cell in a normal adult differential count is the:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Neutrophils typically make up 50-70% of circulating white cells in adults.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Neutrophils primarily function to:
o: Phagocytose bacteria as the first line of cellular defense
Present antigen to T cells primarily
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Neutrophils are phagocytic cells central to acute bacterial defense.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Eosinophils are characteristically increased in:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Eosinophilia is classically associated with helminth infections and allergy/atopy.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Basophils release which mediator important in immediate hypersensitivity reactions?
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Basophils (and mast cells) store and release histamine upon activation.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Monocytes, once they migrate into tissues, differentiate into:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Circulating monocytes become tissue macrophages after extravasation.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Lymphocytes are broadly classified into which major functional groups?
o: T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Lymphocytes comprise T cells, B cells, and NK cells, each with distinct immune roles.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: B lymphocytes mature primarily in the:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: B cells complete maturation in the bone marrow (unlike T cells, which mature in the thymus).

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: T lymphocytes mature in the:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Pre-T cells migrate from marrow to the thymus, where they mature and are selected.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: CD4+ T helper cells primarily function by:
o: Coordinating immune responses via cytokine release and helping B cells/CD8 cells
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Helper T cells orchestrate adaptive immunity through cytokine signaling.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells primarily function to:
o: Present antigen to helper T cells only
Directly kill virus-infected or tumor cells
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Cytotoxic T cells recognize MHC class I-antigen complexes and induce apoptosis in target cells.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, primarily function to:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Plasma cells are antibody factories, the effector form of activated B cells.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Natural killer (NK) cells are part of which arm of immunity?
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: NK cells provide innate, non-specific cytotoxicity against virally infected and tumor cells.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: IgM is characteristically the antibody class:
o: Produced later in a secondary immune response
Produced first in a primary immune response and largest in size (pentamer)
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: IgM is the first antibody made in a primary response, forming a large pentameric molecule.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: IgG is unique among immunoglobulin classes in that it:
o: Crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the fetus/newborn
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: IgG is actively transported across the placenta, conferring passive maternal immunity.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: IgE is primarily responsible for:
o: Agglutinating red cells in transfusion reactions
Mediating immediate (type I) hypersensitivity reactions via mast cell/basophil binding
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: IgE binds Fc receptors on mast cells/basophils, triggering degranulation upon allergen exposure.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Secretory IgA is the predominant immunoglobulin in:
o: Mucosal secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk, gut)
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Dimeric secretory IgA defends mucosal surfaces and is abundant in colostrum.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: The complement system's classical pathway is typically activated by:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: The classical pathway is triggered when C1q binds antibody bound to antigen.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: The membrane attack complex (MAC) of the complement system functions to:
o: Form pores in target cell membranes, causing lysis
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: C5b-C9 assembles into a pore-forming complex that lyses target cells.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Opsonization refers to the process by which:
o: Antibodies are produced by plasma cells
Pathogens are directly lysed by complement
Antigens are presented on MHC molecules
Pathogens are coated with molecules (e.g., antibody, C3b) enhancing phagocytosis
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Opsonins tag pathogens, making them more easily recognized and engulfed by phagocytes.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: MHC class I molecules present antigen to:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Nearly all nucleated cells display MHC I, recognized by CD8+ T cells for surveillance.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: MHC class II molecules are expressed mainly on:
o: Professional antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells)
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: MHC II is restricted largely to professional APCs, presenting to CD4+ T cells.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: The primary function of dendritic cells in the immune system is:
o: Highly efficient antigen presentation to naive T cells, initiating adaptive immunity
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Dendritic cells are the most potent professional antigen-presenting cells, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: A left shift on a peripheral blood smear refers to:
o: A decrease in total white cell count
An increase in immature neutrophil forms (band cells), suggesting acute infection
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: A left shift reflects marrow release of immature band forms during acute bacterial infection.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Neutrophilia (elevated neutrophil count) is most classically associated with:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Acute bacterial infections typically drive neutrophilia.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Lymphocytosis (elevated lymphocyte count) is characteristically seen in:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Viral infections commonly drive a relative and absolute lymphocytosis.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Chemotaxis of neutrophils toward a site of infection is guided mainly by:
o: Chemical gradients of chemoattractants such as complement fragments (C5a) and cytokines
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Neutrophils follow chemoattractant gradients (e.g., C5a, IL-8) to reach infected tissue.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: The primary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes develop and mature, are the:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs for lymphocyte development.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Secondary lymphoid organs, where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen, include the:
o: Spleen, lymph nodes, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Antigen-driven lymphocyte activation occurs in secondary lymphoid tissue.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Cytokines such as interleukins primarily function as:
o: Signaling molecules coordinating immune cell communication
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Cytokines mediate intercellular signaling that shapes immune responses.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Immunological memory, the basis for vaccination, depends primarily on:
o: Long-lived memory B and T cells generated after primary antigen exposure
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Memory lymphocytes persist after infection/vaccination, enabling faster, stronger secondary responses.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Chronic granulomatous disease results from a defect in:
o: Neutrophil/macrophage NADPH oxidase, impairing the respiratory burst
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Defective NADPH oxidase impairs reactive oxygen species production needed for intracellular killing.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Autoimmune disease arises fundamentally from:
o: A breakdown in self-tolerance, causing the immune system to attack self-antigens
Complete absence of an immune system
Excess antibody production against foreign antigens only
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Loss of self-tolerance allows immune attack against the body's own tissues.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: An immediate (type I) hypersensitivity reaction, such as anaphylaxis, is mediated primarily by:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Type I reactions involve IgE cross-linking on mast cells/basophils, triggering rapid mediator release.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: A delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction, such as the tuberculin skin test, is mediated by:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Type IV hypersensitivity is a T cell-mediated response peaking 48-72 hours after antigen exposure.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: The spleen's white pulp is primarily composed of:
o: Lymphoid tissue involved in immune surveillance and response
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: White pulp is lymphoid tissue organized around arterioles, supporting immune responses.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: The spleen's red pulp primarily functions to:
o: Filter and remove aged/defective red blood cells and store platelets
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Red pulp macrophages remove senescent erythrocytes and the spleen reservoir stores platelets.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: A normal total white blood cell count in adults is approximately:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Normal adult WBC counts typically range around 4,000-11,000 cells per microliter.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Interferons are cytokines primarily important in:
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Interferons inhibit viral replication and modulate immune cell activity.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are important pattern recognition receptors of:
o: Innate immunity, recognizing conserved microbial molecular patterns
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: TLRs on innate immune cells detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns, triggering responses.

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.s: Class switching (isotype switching) in B cells allows a single B cell clone to:
o: Change the antibody class produced (e.g., IgM to IgG) while retaining antigen specificity
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.e: Class switching alters the antibody's constant region/effector function without changing its variable region specificity.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: The first response to vascular injury in hemostasis is:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Immediate vasoconstriction reduces blood flow and loss at the injury site.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen is mediated primarily via:
o: Von Willebrand factor bridging platelet GPIb receptors to collagen
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Von Willebrand factor bridges platelets to exposed collagen, initiating adhesion.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Platelet aggregation is primarily mediated by fibrinogen binding to which receptor?
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Activated GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen, cross-linking platelets during aggregation.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Which substance released from activated platelets promotes further platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction?
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Thromboxane A2 promotes platelet aggregation and local vasoconstriction.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Prostacyclin (PGI2), produced by endothelial cells, functions to:
o: Inhibit platelet aggregation and cause vasodilation
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Prostacyclin counterbalances thromboxane, limiting unwanted platelet activation in healthy endothelium.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: The extrinsic pathway of coagulation is initiated by:
o: Tissue factor (factor III) released from damaged tissue, activating factor VII
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Tissue factor exposed at injury sites activates factor VII, starting the extrinsic pathway.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: The intrinsic pathway of coagulation is initiated by contact activation involving:
o: Factor XII (Hageman factor) contacting exposed subendothelial collagen
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Factor XII activation upon contact with negatively charged surfaces begins the intrinsic pathway.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: The common pathway of coagulation begins with activation of:
o: Factor X, leading to prothrombin conversion to thrombin
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Activated factor X converts prothrombin to thrombin, the shared final common pathway step.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Thrombin's key roles in coagulation include converting fibrinogen to fibrin and:
o: Activating platelets and factors V, VIII, and XIII
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Thrombin amplifies coagulation by activating platelets and several clotting factors.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Factor XIII functions to:
o: Cross-link fibrin monomers, stabilizing the clot
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin strands, converting a soft clot into a stable, insoluble mesh.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Vitamin K is required for the synthesis of functional forms of which clotting factors?
o: Factors II, VII, IX, and X (and proteins C and S)
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Vitamin K enables gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C/S.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Warfarin exerts its anticoagulant effect by:
o: Inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, reducing functional clotting factor synthesis.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Heparin's anticoagulant effect is mediated by:
o: Potentiating antithrombin III, which inactivates thrombin and factor Xa
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Heparin markedly accelerates antithrombin III's inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Aspirin's antiplatelet effect results from:
o: Irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), reducing thromboxane A2 production
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, decreasing thromboxane A2 synthesis in platelets.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Protein C, once activated, functions to:
o: Inactivate factors Va and VIIIa, acting as a natural anticoagulant
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Activated protein C (with protein S) degrades factors Va/VIIIa, limiting clot propagation.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Antithrombin III is a natural anticoagulant that primarily inhibits:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Antithrombin III neutralizes thrombin and activated factor X, limiting coagulation.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Plasmin's principal function in hemostasis is to:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Plasmin breaks down fibrin polymers, dissolving clots once healing is underway.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) functions to:
o: Convert plasminogen to active plasmin, promoting fibrinolysis
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: tPA cleaves plasminogen to plasmin, the key enzyme of clot breakdown.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: D-dimer, a laboratory marker used to assess for thrombosis, is a degradation product of:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: D-dimer specifically results from plasmin degrading cross-linked fibrin, indicating recent clot formation and breakdown.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Hemophilia A results from deficiency of:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Hemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) results from deficiency of:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Hemophilia B is caused by deficient factor IX.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, primarily impairs:
o: Platelet adhesion and factor VIII stability
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Deficient/dysfunctional vWF impairs platelet adhesion and destabilizes circulating factor VIII.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Prothrombin time (PT) is primarily used to assess the:
o: Extrinsic and common pathways (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen)
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: PT is sensitive to extrinsic and common pathway factors and monitors warfarin therapy.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) primarily assesses the:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: aPTT screens intrinsic and common pathway factors and monitors heparin therapy.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is characterized by:
o: Widespread activation of coagulation, consuming platelets and clotting factors, causing both clotting and bleeding
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: DIC consumes clotting factors and platelets systemically, paradoxically causing bleeding despite widespread clot formation.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Thrombocytopenia is defined as a platelet count below approximately:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: A platelet count under roughly 150,000/microL defines thrombocytopenia.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Normal platelet count in adults is approximately:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Normal platelet counts range roughly from 150,000 to 450,000 per microliter.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: The average lifespan of a circulating platelet is approximately:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Platelets circulate for roughly 8-10 days before removal, mainly by the spleen.
