blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Clot retraction, which helps approximate wound edges, depends primarily on:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Platelet contractile proteins pull on the fibrin mesh, retracting and consolidating the clot.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Calcium ion (factor IV) is essential in coagulation because it:
o: Is required as a cofactor for several clotting factor complexes to assemble on phospholipid surfaces
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Calcium bridges gamma-carboxylated clotting factors to phospholipid surfaces, enabling complex assembly.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Citrate is used as an anticoagulant in blood collection tubes because it:
o: Chelates calcium, preventing coagulation factor complex assembly
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Citrate binds free calcium, which is required for coagulation cascade reactions.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from a deficiency of:
o: GPIb receptor, impairing platelet adhesion to von Willebrand factor
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Bernard-Soulier syndrome involves defective GPIb, impairing platelet adhesion via vWF.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Glanzmann thrombasthenia results from a deficiency of:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Absent/defective GPIIb/IIIa prevents fibrinogen-mediated platelet-to-platelet aggregation.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Fresh frozen plasma transfusion is used clinically primarily to:
o: Replace multiple clotting factors in patients with coagulopathy
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: FFP contains all plasma clotting factors, useful for correcting multifactorial coagulopathy.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Bleeding time (or platelet function assays) primarily reflects abnormalities of:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Bleeding time (historically) and modern platelet function tests assess primary hemostasis (platelets/vessel wall).

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Endothelial cells normally maintain blood fluidity by producing:
o: Von Willebrand factor without any inhibitory factors
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Healthy endothelium secretes anticoagulant/antiplatelet substances to maintain vascular patency.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Thrombomodulin on endothelial cells functions to:
o: Bind thrombin and convert it into an activator of protein C
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin switches roles, activating protein C rather than promoting clotting.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Massive transfusion protocols aim to replace blood components in a ratio approximating whole blood mainly to prevent:
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Balanced transfusion of red cells, plasma, and platelets helps avoid dilutional coagulopathy in massive hemorrhage.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: Low molecular weight heparin differs from unfractionated heparin mainly in that it:
o: Works by an entirely different, non-antithrombin mechanism
Has more predictable pharmacokinetics and predominantly inhibits factor Xa
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: LMWH has a more predictable dose-response, mainly potentiating antithrombin's action against factor Xa.

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.s: A prolonged aPTT that corrects with a mixing study (patient plus normal plasma) suggests:
o: A factor deficiency (correctable by replacing the missing factor)
blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.e: Correction on mixing indicates the prolongation is due to a missing factor, not an inhibitor.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: The ABO blood group antigens are located on the:
o: Surface of red blood cells (and other tissues)
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: ABO antigens are glycoproteins/glycolipids expressed on the RBC membrane surface.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: A person with blood group A has which antibodies in their plasma (naturally occurring)?
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Group A individuals lack A antigen recognition issues but naturally form anti-B antibodies.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: A person with blood group O is often called the universal donor for red cells because their cells:
o: Have both A and B antigens
Lack both A and B antigens on red cells
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: O red cells lack A and B antigens, reducing the risk of ABO-mediated transfusion reaction in recipients.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Blood group AB individuals are often called universal recipients because their plasma:
o: Contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: AB individuals lack anti-A/anti-B antibodies, allowing them to receive any ABO type of red cells (with Rh compatibility).

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: The Rh(D) antigen is clinically significant primarily because:
o: It is present on all humans universally
Rh-negative individuals can form anti-D antibodies after exposure to Rh-positive blood, risking hemolytic reactions
It never causes hemolytic disease of the newborn
It is only relevant in blood banking, not pregnancy
It is identical to the ABO antigen
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Rh-negative individuals sensitized to D antigen can produce anti-D, risking future transfusion reactions or HDN.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Hemolytic disease of the newborn due to Rh incompatibility typically occurs when:
o: An Rh-positive mother carries an Rh-negative fetus
An Rh-negative mother, previously sensitized, carries an Rh-positive fetus
The mother is blood group O
The fetus is blood group AB
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Maternal anti-D antibodies (from prior sensitization) cross the placenta and hemolyze Rh-positive fetal red cells.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) is given to Rh-negative mothers to:
o: Treat existing hemolytic disease of the newborn
Prevent maternal sensitization to the Rh(D) antigen from fetal red cells
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: RhoGAM neutralizes fetal Rh-positive cells before the maternal immune system can mount a sensitizing response.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: A major crossmatch before transfusion tests for compatibility between:
o: Recipient serum/plasma and donor red cells
Donor red cells and donor red cells from another unit
Recipient red cells and recipient plasma
Donor plasma and donor red cells
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: The major crossmatch checks whether recipient antibodies would react against donor red cells.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction due to ABO incompatibility is caused by:
o: Excess citrate in the transfused blood
Allergic reaction to plasma proteins only
Pre-formed recipient antibodies rapidly destroying transfused incompatible red cells
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Pre-existing ABO antibodies cause rapid intravascular hemolysis of mismatched donor cells.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Iron deficiency anemia is classically characterized by:
o: Microcytic, hypochromic red cells with low serum ferritin
Macrocytic red cells with hypersegmented neutrophils
Normocytic red cells with high reticulocyte count
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Iron deficiency limits hemoglobin synthesis, producing small, pale (microcytic, hypochromic) red cells.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Megaloblastic anemia (B12/folate deficiency) is classically characterized by:
o: Normal-sized red cells with high reticulocyte count
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Impaired DNA synthesis produces large, immature red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Aplastic anemia results from:
o: Bone marrow failure, causing pancytopenia (reduced red cells, white cells, and platelets)
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Aplastic anemia reflects marrow failure affecting all three cell lines, not an isolated red cell problem.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Hemolytic anemia is characterized biochemically by:
o: Decreased unconjugated bilirubin and decreased LDH
Normal LDH and bilirubin with low haptoglobin
Increased serum ferritin exclusively as diagnostic
Increased unconjugated bilirubin, increased LDH, and decreased haptoglobin
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Red cell breakdown raises unconjugated bilirubin and LDH while consuming haptoglobin, which binds free hemoglobin.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Chronic kidney disease commonly causes anemia primarily due to:
o: Reduced erythropoietin production by damaged kidneys
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Diseased kidneys produce insufficient erythropoietin, blunting red cell production.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: A blood smear showing target cells is most classically associated with:
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Target cells reflect an increased membrane-to-volume ratio, seen in thalassemia, liver disease, and post-splenectomy states.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is caused by:
o: Autoantibodies directed against the patient's own red blood cell antigens
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Autoantibodies bind self red cells, triggering complement-mediated or macrophage-mediated destruction.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: A positive direct Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test indicates:
o: Presence of antibody or complement bound to the patient's own red blood cells
Presence of free antibody in plasma only
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: The direct Coombs test detects antibody/complement already coating the patient's circulating red cells.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: G6PD deficiency predisposes to hemolysis primarily under conditions of:
o: Oxidative stress (e.g., certain drugs, fava beans, infection)
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: G6PD deficiency impairs the cell's antioxidant defenses, causing hemolysis under oxidative stress.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Anemia due to chronic blood loss (e.g., GI bleeding) typically presents similarly to:
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Chronic blood loss depletes iron stores over time, producing an iron-deficiency picture.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Packed red blood cell transfusion is primarily indicated to:
o: Increase oxygen-carrying capacity in symptomatic anemia or significant blood loss
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: PRBC transfusion restores hemoglobin/oxygen-carrying capacity, not clotting factors or platelets.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Anemia of prematurity and physiological anemia of infancy relate mainly to:
o: A normal postnatal drop in erythropoietin as fetal hemoglobin is replaced and oxygen delivery improves
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: After birth, improved oxygenation lowers erythropoietin, causing a physiological nadir in hemoglobin around 2-3 months.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Blood group inheritance follows a genetic system where A and B alleles are:
o: Codominant to each other and dominant over O
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: A and B alleles are codominant and both dominant over the recessive O allele.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: The Bombay phenotype results from:
o: Absence of the H antigen, preventing expression of A or B antigens despite the underlying genotype
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Without the H antigen precursor, A/B antigens cannot be built even if those genes are present.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Platelet transfusions are primarily indicated for:
o: Significant thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction with bleeding/high bleeding risk
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Platelet concentrates address low platelet counts or dysfunction, not anemia or plasma factor deficiency.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Cryoprecipitate is rich in which coagulation components?
o: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and factor XIII
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Cryoprecipitate concentrates these specific plasma proteins from fresh frozen plasma.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is thought to result from:
o: Donor antibodies reacting with recipient leukocytes, causing pulmonary capillary leak
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: TRALI is thought to involve donor anti-leukocyte antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in the lung.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: A febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is most often caused by:
o: Recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte antigens or cytokines in stored blood
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: This common, milder reaction is linked to leukocyte antibodies or accumulated cytokines in stored components.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: A delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction typically occurs due to:
o: An anamnestic antibody response to a minor blood group antigen days after transfusion
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: A prior sensitization to a minor antigen can cause a delayed secondary antibody response days later.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: According to WHO criteria, anemia in adult non-pregnant women is generally defined as hemoglobin below approximately:
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: WHO defines anemia in non-pregnant women as hemoglobin below about 12 g/dL.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Anemia can be broadly classified by mechanism into decreased production, increased destruction, and:
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: The three broad mechanistic categories of anemia are underproduction, increased destruction, and blood loss.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: The reticulocyte production index helps distinguish:
o: Whether anemia reflects an appropriate marrow response or inadequate production
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: A corrected reticulocyte index shows whether marrow output is appropriately elevated for the degree of anemia.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Beta-thalassemia trait (heterozygous) typically presents with:
o: Mild microcytic anemia, often asymptomatic, with normal or near-normal hemoglobin
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Trait (heterozygous) carriers usually have mild, often incidental microcytosis without significant anemia.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Physiological anemia of pregnancy results mainly from:
o: True iron deficiency in all cases
Plasma volume expansion exceeding the increase in red cell mass (hemodilution)
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Pregnancy increases plasma volume proportionally more than red cell mass, causing dilutional anemia.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Cold agglutinin disease is typically mediated by which antibody class binding red cells at low temperature?
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: IgM cold agglutinins bind red cells preferentially at lower peripheral temperatures.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is typically mediated by which antibody class?
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Warm AIHA is classically IgG-mediated, reacting optimally at body temperature.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Leukoreduction filters are used on blood products primarily to reduce the risk of:
o: Febrile non-hemolytic reactions and cytomegalovirus transmission
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Removing leukocytes lowers febrile reaction risk and reduces leukocyte-associated viral transmission risk.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Packed red blood cells are typically stored (refrigerated) for a shelf life of approximately:
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: With standard additive solutions, PRBCs are generally usable for about 35-42 days refrigerated.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Minor blood group systems such as Kell, Duffy, and Kidd are clinically significant mainly because:
o: They only matter in platelet transfusion
Antibodies against them can cause delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions or hemolytic disease of the newborn
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Sensitization to minor antigens can cause delayed transfusion reactions or contribute to HDN.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: The common clinical signs of anemia (pallor, fatigue, tachycardia) result primarily from:
o: Excess red cell destruction visible on skin
Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity leading to tissue hypoxia and compensatory cardiovascular response
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Anemia symptoms reflect the body's response to inadequate tissue oxygen delivery.

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.s: Peripheral blood smear examination is a key initial step in anemia workup because it can reveal:
o: Red cell size, shape, and inclusions that narrow the differential diagnosis
blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.e: Smear morphology (e.g., microcytes, spherocytes, target cells) provides diagnostic clues beyond automated counts.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The primary function of the lymphatic system includes:
o: Digesting fats exclusively without transport role
Returning interstitial fluid to the venous circulation and immune surveillance
Producing red blood cells in adults
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Lymphatics drain excess interstitial fluid, proteins, and (in the gut) chylomicrons back to the bloodstream, alongside immune functions.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Lymph ultimately drains into the venous system primarily via the:
o: Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein (and right lymphatic duct into the right)
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The thoracic duct empties into the left venous angle; the right lymphatic duct drains the right upper body.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The thoracic duct drains lymph from:
o: Only the right arm and right side of the head/neck
The majority of the body: lower limbs, abdomen, left thorax, left arm, and left head/neck
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The thoracic duct is the major lymphatic trunk draining most of the body below the diaphragm plus the left upper quadrant.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Lacteals are specialized lymphatic capillaries found in the:
o: Small intestinal villi, absorbing dietary lipids as chylomicrons
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Lacteals absorb dietary fat (as chylomicrons) from the intestinal villi into the lymphatic system.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: A lymph node's cortex primarily contains:
o: B cell-rich lymphoid follicles (some with germinal centers)
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The outer cortex contains B cell follicles, often with germinal centers during active immune responses.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The paracortex of a lymph node is primarily populated by:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The deep cortex (paracortex) is a T cell-dependent zone.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Afferent lymphatic vessels enter a lymph node at the:
o: Convex surface, draining into the subcapsular sinus
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Multiple afferent lymphatics pierce the capsule at the convex surface, emptying into the subcapsular sinus.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Efferent lymphatic vessels leave a lymph node at the:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: A single (or few) efferent vessel exits at the hilum, along with blood vessels.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The medulla of a lymph node contains medullary cords rich in:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Medullary cords house antibody-secreting plasma cells and macrophages that filter lymph.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The tonsils, part of Waldeyer's ring, are classified as:
o: Secondary lymphoid tissue without a complete capsule
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Tonsils are partially encapsulated mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue guarding the pharynx.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Peyer's patches, aggregates of lymphoid tissue in the gut, are most concentrated in the:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Peyer's patches are prominent lymphoid aggregates in the ileal submucosa, sampling luminal antigens.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: M cells overlying Peyer's patches primarily function to:
o: Transport (sample) luminal antigens to underlying immune cells
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: M cells transcytose antigens from the gut lumen to underlying lymphoid tissue, initiating mucosal immunity.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The thymus is most active (largest relative to body size) during:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The thymus is proportionally largest in childhood and progressively involutes into fatty tissue with age.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The thymic cortex is densely populated with:
o: Immature, proliferating T lymphocytes (thymocytes) undergoing positive selection
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The thymic cortex is where immature thymocytes proliferate and undergo positive selection.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Hassall's corpuscles, characteristic structures of the thymus, are located in the:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Hassall's corpuscles are whorled epithelial structures found in the thymic medulla.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Negative selection of T lymphocytes, eliminating strongly self-reactive clones, occurs mainly in the:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Medullary thymic epithelial cells present self-antigens, allowing deletion of strongly autoreactive T cells.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Lymphedema results from:
o: Impaired lymphatic drainage, causing protein-rich fluid accumulation in tissue
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Blocked or damaged lymphatics fail to clear interstitial fluid/protein, causing swelling.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Splenectomy predisposes patients to infection especially with encapsulated organisms because the spleen normally:
o: Produces all antibodies in the body
Filters only red blood cells, not bacteria
Provides major clearance of encapsulated bacteria via opsonization and phagocytosis
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The spleen is critical for clearing poorly opsonized encapsulated bacteria from the blood.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries in that they:
o: Have a complete, continuous basement membrane like blood capillaries
Are blind-ended with overlapping endothelial cells acting as one-way flap valves
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended, highly permeable vessels with valve-like endothelial junctions allowing one-way fluid entry.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) is important because it:
o: Provides localized immune defense at mucosal surfaces exposed to the external environment
Replaces the need for the spleen
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: MALT (gut, bronchus, etc.) provides frontline immune surveillance at mucosal barriers.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The cisterna chyli, the dilated origin of the thoracic duct, is typically located at the level of:
o: L1-L2 vertebrae, anterior to the lumbar vertebrae
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The cisterna chyli lies anterior to the L1-L2 vertebral bodies, receiving lumbar and intestinal lymph trunks.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from:
o: The right upper limb, right side of the head/neck, and right thorax
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The right lymphatic duct handles only the right upper quadrant of the body.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Lymph flow through lymphatic vessels is propelled mainly by:
o: Skeletal muscle contraction, one-way valves, and rhythmic contraction of lymphatic vessel walls
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Lacking a central pump, lymph relies on the muscle pump, valves, and intrinsic vessel contractility.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Lymphangitis, inflammation of lymphatic vessels often from bacterial infection, classically presents as:
o: Painless swelling of the whole limb
Red streaking along the course of lymphatic vessels toward regional nodes
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Infection tracking along lymphatics produces characteristic tender red streaking toward draining nodes.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The concept of a sentinel lymph node is used clinically to:
o: Identify the first lymph node(s) draining a tumor site, guiding staging (e.g., in breast cancer)
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The sentinel node is the first to receive tumor drainage, so its status guides staging and further treatment.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: High endothelial venules, specialized vessels found in lymph nodes, primarily function to:
o: Drain lymph out of the node
Allow circulating lymphocytes to migrate from blood into the lymph node parenchyma
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: HEVs are the specialized site of lymphocyte extravasation from blood into lymph nodes.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Germinal centers within lymphoid follicles are sites of:
o: B cell proliferation, somatic hypermutation, and affinity maturation
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Germinal centers are where activated B cells proliferate and refine antibody affinity.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The marginal zone of the splenic white pulp is important for:
o: Capturing blood-borne antigens and initiating rapid immune responses, especially to encapsulated bacteria
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The marginal zone is strategically positioned to sample blood-borne antigens for rapid immune activation.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Splenic red pulp sinusoids have a discontinuous ('barrel-hoop') endothelial lining that functions to:
o: Allow red blood cells to squeeze through, testing their deformability, and remove less deformable/aged cells
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: This unique architecture 'quality-checks' red cell flexibility, culling aged or damaged cells.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The thymus develops embryologically from the:
o: Third pharyngeal pouch (and third pharyngeal cleft contributions)
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The thymus arises mainly from the third pharyngeal pouch endoderm.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The spleen develops embryologically within the:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The spleen forms within a fold of the dorsal mesogastrium, explaining its intraperitoneal position.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Lymphocyte recirculation, the continuous movement of lymphocytes between blood, lymph, and lymphoid tissue, primarily serves to:
o: Maximize the chance that antigen-specific lymphocytes encounter their specific antigen
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Continuous surveillance increases the odds that rare antigen-specific clones meet their antigen.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT) provides localized immune defense in the:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: BALT is the airway-associated counterpart of gut MALT, guarding the respiratory mucosa.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The three types of tonsils forming Waldeyer's ring include the palatine, lingual, and:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Waldeyer's ring comprises the palatine, lingual, and pharyngeal (adenoid) tonsils, plus tubal tonsils.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Clinically, breast cancer most commonly metastasizes first to which lymph node group?
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Most breast lymphatic drainage passes through axillary nodes, making them the first common metastatic site.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Accessory spleens (splenunculi) are:
o: Small, congenitally normal variants of splenic tissue found near the main spleen
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Accessory spleens are common, usually incidental congenital variants near the splenic hilum.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The splenic artery is a branch of the:
o: Aorta directly, unrelated to the celiac trunk
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: The splenic artery is one of the three main branches of the celiac trunk.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Splenomegaly can result from conditions including portal hypertension and:
o: Hemolytic anemias and infections (e.g., malaria, infectious mononucleosis)
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Congestion, increased red cell destruction workload, and infection are common causes of splenic enlargement.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: The primary immune function of MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) throughout the body is to:
o: Provide a first line of adaptive immune defense at mucosal surfaces exposed to the environment
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: MALT surveils and responds to antigens encountered at mucosal barriers throughout the body.

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.s: Chyle, the lymph draining from intestinal lacteals, appears milky white due to its high content of:
blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.e: Absorbed dietary lipids packaged as chylomicrons give intestinal lymph its characteristic milky appearance.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerves?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The brachial plexus arises from C5-T1 ventral rami.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The five terminal branches of the brachial plexus include the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, ulnar, and:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The median nerve is the fifth terminal branch of the brachial plexus.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The axillary nerve is most at risk of injury in which condition?
o: Fracture of the hook of hamate
Anterior dislocation of the shoulder or surgical neck fracture of the humerus
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck, close to the shoulder joint.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Axillary nerve injury classically results in:
o: Deltoid paralysis and loss of sensation over the 'regimental badge' area
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and skin over the lower deltoid.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The radial nerve is most commonly injured in association with fracture of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The radial nerve runs in the radial (spiral) groove of the humeral shaft.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Radial nerve injury classically presents with:
o: Wrist drop (inability to extend the wrist and fingers)
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The radial nerve supplies the extensor compartment of the forearm.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The median nerve is most vulnerable to injury at the wrist in:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist, vulnerable to compression.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Carpal tunnel syndrome classically presents with sensory disturbance over which digits?
o: The medial one and a half digits
The lateral three and a half digits (thumb, index, middle, half of ring finger)
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The median nerve supplies sensation to the lateral three and a half digits.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The ulnar nerve is most commonly injured at the:
o: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (cubital tunnel)
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle, exposed to injury there.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Ulnar nerve injury classically produces a deformity described as:
o: Claw hand (hyperextension at MCP joints, flexion at IP joints of ring and little fingers)
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Loss of ulnar-innervated intrinsic hand muscles produces the classic ulnar claw.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The musculocutaneous nerve innervates the muscles of the:
o: Anterior compartment of the arm (biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis)
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm flexor compartment.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Erb's palsy results from injury to which part of the brachial plexus?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Erb's palsy involves traction injury to the C5-C6 upper trunk.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Erb's palsy classically produces the 'waiter's tip' position due to weakness of muscles including the:
o: Deltoid, biceps, and shoulder external rotators
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Loss of C5-C6 innervated muscles produces adduction/medial rotation of the arm and pronated forearm.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Klumpke's palsy results from injury to which part of the brachial plexus?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Klumpke's palsy involves the C8-T1 lower trunk, often from upward traction on an abducted arm.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Klumpke's palsy classically produces:
o: Claw hand due to intrinsic hand muscle paralysis
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Loss of C8-T1 innervated intrinsic hand muscles produces a claw hand.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The rotator cuff is composed of four muscles: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Subscapularis is the fourth rotator cuff muscle (SITS mnemonic).

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The rotator cuff muscle most commonly torn/injured is the:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Supraspinatus is most vulnerable due to its course under the acromion and relatively poor blood supply zone.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The long head of the biceps brachii tendon passes through the:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The long head tendon runs in the intertubercular groove between greater and lesser tubercles.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The axillary artery is a continuation of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The brachial artery typically bifurcates into the radial and ulnar arteries at the level of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Bifurcation classically occurs just distal to the elbow, in the cubital fossa.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The boundaries of the cubital fossa include the brachioradialis laterally and which muscle medially?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Pronator teres forms the medial border of the cubital fossa.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: In the cubital fossa, from lateral to medial the order of structures is:
o: Radial nerve, brachial artery, median nerve
Biceps brachii tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
Brachial artery, median nerve, biceps tendon
Median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon
Median nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Lateral to medial: biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve (TAN mnemonic).

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The anatomical snuffbox is bordered by the tendons of extensor pollicis longus and:
o: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: These thumb tendons form the borders of the anatomical snuffbox.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The radial artery is palpable within the anatomical snuffbox and at the:
o: Wrist, lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The radial pulse is classically palpated at the wrist just lateral to flexor carpi radialis.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The scaphoid is the carpal bone most commonly fractured, typically from a:
o: Direct blow to the dorsum of the hand
Twisting injury of the wrist only
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: FOOSH injuries transmit force through the wrist, commonly fracturing the scaphoid.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: A scaphoid fracture carries a risk of avascular necrosis because its blood supply:
o: Enters proximally and flows distally, generously
Is derived entirely from venous return
Enters distally and flows retrograde proximally, which can be disrupted by a fracture
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Retrograde blood flow means proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The hook of hamate is clinically relevant because it can compress which nerve in Guyon's canal?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The ulnar nerve and artery pass through Guyon's canal near the hook of hamate.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The suprascapular nerve innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, arising from the:
o: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The suprascapular nerve branches directly from the upper trunk.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Winging of the scapula is classically caused by paralysis of the serratus anterior due to injury of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The long thoracic nerve innervates serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the thorax.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The thoracodorsal nerve innervates which muscle, relevant in axillary lymph node dissection?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The thoracodorsal nerve runs with the subscapular vessels to latissimus dorsi, at risk during axillary surgery.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint is classified as a:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The shoulder is a highly mobile ball-and-socket joint, at the cost of stability.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The elbow joint primarily allows which type of movement?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The humeroulnar joint functions as a hinge, allowing flexion/extension.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The proximal and distal radioulnar joints together allow:
o: Pronation and supination of the forearm
Flexion and extension of the elbow
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: These pivot joints allow the radius to rotate around the ulna, producing pronation/supination.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is classified as which type of synovial joint?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The wrist is a condyloid joint, allowing flexion/extension and abduction/adduction.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is classified as a:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The trapezium-first metacarpal saddle joint uniquely allows thumb opposition.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: Sensory innervation of the lateral (radial) side of the dorsum of the hand is primarily supplied by the:
o: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The superficial radial nerve supplies the dorsolateral hand skin.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The dermatome for the thumb (C6) is clinically tested to assess the integrity of which nerve root?
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The thumb corresponds to the C6 dermatome.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The biceps reflex primarily tests the integrity of nerve roots:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The biceps reflex is mediated by the musculocutaneous nerve, C5-C6.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The triceps reflex primarily tests the integrity of nerve root:
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: The triceps reflex, via the radial nerve, primarily reflects C7 integrity.

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.s: The axillary lymph nodes primarily drain lymph from the:
o: Upper limb, breast, and lateral thoracic wall
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.e: Axillary nodes are the principal drainage site for the upper limb and breast.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The lumbosacral plexus contributing to the lower limb arises from ventral rami of:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The lower limb is innervated via the lumbar and sacral plexuses, spanning T12-S4.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The femoral nerve arises from the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The femoral nerve is the largest branch of the lumbar plexus.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The femoral nerve innervates the muscles of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh extensor compartment.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The sciatic nerve arises from which nerve roots?
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The sciatic nerve, the body's largest nerve, arises from L4-S3.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The sciatic nerve divides into its two terminal branches, the tibial and common fibular (peroneal) nerves, typically at the level of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Division classically occurs near the apex of the popliteal fossa, though it can be higher.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: Injury to the common fibular (peroneal) nerve classically results in:
o: Foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion) and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The common fibular nerve supplies the anterior/lateral leg compartments (dorsiflexors).

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The common fibular nerve is particularly vulnerable to injury as it winds around the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Its superficial course around the fibular neck makes it prone to compression injury.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The tibial nerve innervates the muscles of the:
o: Posterior compartment of the leg (calf muscles)
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The tibial nerve supplies the posterior leg (plantarflexor) compartment.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: Injury to the tibial nerve results primarily in:
o: Loss of plantarflexion and inversion, with sensory loss on the sole of the foot
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Tibial nerve loss impairs plantarflexion and sole sensation.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The obturator nerve, arising from the lumbar plexus, innervates the muscles of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The obturator nerve supplies the hip adductor muscle group.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The superior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus medius and minimus; its injury classically causes:
o: A positive Trendelenburg sign (pelvic drop on the contralateral side during single-leg stance)
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Loss of hip abductor function produces a Trendelenburg gait.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The inferior gluteal nerve is dedicated to gluteus maximus.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The femoral triangle's boundaries include the inguinal ligament superiorly, sartorius laterally, and which muscle medially?
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Adductor longus forms the medial border of the femoral triangle.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: From lateral to medial, the contents of the femoral triangle are classically remembered as:
o: Nerve, Artery, Vein (NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics)
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: NAVEL mnemonic gives the lateral-to-medial order in the femoral triangle.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The femoral pulse is palpated at the midpoint of the:
o: Groin crease laterally near the ASIS
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The femoral pulse is found at the midinguinal point, halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The popliteal artery is a continuation of the:
o: Femoral artery, after passing through the adductor hiatus
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery after traversing the adductor hiatus.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The dorsalis pedis artery, palpable on the dorsum of the foot, is a continuation of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The anterior tibial artery continues onto the dorsum of the foot as dorsalis pedis.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The posterior tibial pulse is classically palpated:
o: On the dorsum of the foot
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The hip joint is classified as a:
o: Ball-and-socket synovial joint, deeper and more stable than the shoulder
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The deep acetabulum gives the hip more inherent stability than the shoulder.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The knee joint primarily allows which movement, along with some rotation when flexed?
o: Flexion and extension (a modified hinge joint)
Abduction and adduction as the main movement
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The knee is a modified hinge joint, permitting flexion/extension and some rotation when flexed.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) of the knee primarily functions to prevent:
o: Posterior displacement of the tibia on the femur
Anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The ACL resists anterior tibial translation relative to the femur.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) primarily prevents:
o: Posterior displacement of the tibia on the femur
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The PCL resists posterior tibial translation.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The medial and lateral menisci of the knee function primarily to:
o: Absorb shock and improve congruity between femoral and tibial condyles
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Menisci cushion load and deepen the tibial articular surface for the femoral condyles.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The ankle (talocrural) joint is classified as a:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The talocrural joint acts as a hinge for dorsiflexion/plantarflexion.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: Inversion and eversion of the foot occur mainly at the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The subtalar (talocalcaneal) joint is responsible for inversion/eversion.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The medial longitudinal arch of the foot is supported primarily by the:
o: Deltoid ligament, spring ligament, and tibialis posterior tendon
Only bony architecture with no soft tissue support
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Ligamentous and tendinous supports, not bone alone, maintain the medial arch.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The Achilles (calcaneal) tendon is the common insertion of which muscles?
o: Tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Gastrocnemius and soleus form the triceps surae, inserting via the Achilles tendon.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The sural nerve, commonly used for nerve biopsy, provides sensation to the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The sural nerve is a superficial sensory nerve of the posterolateral leg/lateral foot.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, supplies sensation to the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The saphenous nerve is the femoral nerve's terminal cutaneous branch to the medial leg/foot.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The greater saphenous vein, commonly used for coronary artery bypass grafts, runs:
o: Along the lateral leg to drain into the popliteal vein
Anterior to the medial malleolus, up the medial leg and thigh, draining into the femoral vein
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The great saphenous vein is a superficial vein running the length of the medial leg and thigh.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The patella is classified functionally as a:
o: Sesamoid bone within the quadriceps tendon
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The patella is the largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The Q-angle of the knee, relevant to patellar tracking, is measured between the:
o: Femur and tibia only in the sagittal plane
Line from ASIS to patella center and line from patella center to tibial tuberosity
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The Q-angle assesses the lateral pull vector on the patella.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: Injury to the L4 nerve root classically affects which reflex?
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The patellar (knee jerk) reflex primarily tests L3-L4, with L4 most emphasized clinically.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The ankle jerk (Achilles) reflex primarily tests nerve root(s):
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: The Achilles reflex is mediated primarily by S1 (with S2 contribution).

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The gluteus maximus is the primary muscle for:
o: Hip extension, especially from a flexed position (e.g., climbing stairs)
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Gluteus maximus is the chief hip extensor, especially powerful from flexion.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: Iliopsoas (iliacus and psoas major) is the primary muscle for:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Iliopsoas is the strongest hip flexor.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The quadriceps femoris muscle group's primary action is:
o: Knee extension (with rectus femoris also flexing the hip)
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Quadriceps femoris is the principal knee extensor group.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The hamstring muscle group (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) primarily produces:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Hamstrings flex the knee and extend the hip.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: Deep vein thrombosis most commonly occurs in which lower limb vessels?
o: Deep veins of the calf (e.g., posterior tibial, soleal veins)
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Deep calf veins are the classic site of origin for lower limb DVT.

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.s: The inguinal lymph nodes primarily drain lymph from the:
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.e: Inguinal nodes are the principal drainage site for the lower limb and perineum.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The vertebral column typically consists of how many presacral vertebrae?
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: 24 presacral vertebrae, plus the fused sacrum and coccyx, make up the column.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The first cervical vertebra (atlas) is unique in that it:
o: Lacks a body and spinous process, articulating with the occipital condyles
Has a large body and spinous process
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The atlas is ring-shaped, lacking a vertebral body, supporting the skull.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The second cervical vertebra (axis) is characterized by the presence of the:
o: Dens (odontoid process), around which the atlas rotates
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The dens projects superiorly from the axis body, forming a pivot for atlantoaxial rotation.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Atlanto-axial rotation (turning the head side to side) primarily occurs at the:
o: Atlanto-axial joint (pivot joint around the dens)
Intervertebral discs of the thoracic spine
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The atlas rotates around the dens at the atlantoaxial joint.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Flexion and extension of the head ('yes' movement) occur primarily at the:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The occipital condyles rock on the atlas at the atlanto-occipital joint, producing nodding.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Thoracic vertebrae are distinguished by the presence of:
o: A large vertebral foramen relative to body size
Costal facets for articulation with ribs
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Costal facets on the body and transverse processes uniquely identify thoracic vertebrae.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Cervical vertebrae are distinguished by the presence of:
o: Transverse foramina, transmitting the vertebral artery
Long, non-bifid spinous processes in all cervical vertebrae
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Transverse foramina carrying the vertebral vessels are unique to cervical vertebrae.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The spinal cord in adults typically terminates (conus medullaris) at approximately the level of:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The adult cord ends around L1-L2 due to differential growth of the vertebral column.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Lumbar puncture is typically performed below the level of the spinal cord termination, most commonly at the:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Below L2, only the cauda equina occupies the canal, making puncture safer.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The intervertebral disc is composed of a central nucleus pulposus and a surrounding:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The anulus fibrosus is the tough outer ring containing the gel-like nucleus pulposus.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Herniation of the nucleus pulposus most commonly occurs in which direction, potentially compressing a nerve root?
o: Posterolaterally, into the intervertebral foramen or spinal canal
Laterally away from the canal only
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The posterior longitudinal ligament is relatively weaker posterolaterally, favoring herniation there.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The ligamentum flavum connects adjacent vertebral:
o: Laminae, and is pierced during epidural anesthesia
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The ligamentum flavum links laminae of adjacent vertebrae, providing a landmark for epidural needle placement.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The anterior longitudinal ligament runs along the:
o: Posterior surface of vertebral bodies only
Anterior surface of vertebral bodies, preventing hyperextension
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: This ligament limits excessive extension of the vertebral column.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The posterior longitudinal ligament runs along the:
o: Posterior surface of vertebral bodies (within the vertebral canal), limiting hyperflexion and disc herniation anteriorly
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: It lines the posterior vertebral bodies within the canal, resisting flexion and central disc herniation.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The spinal cord is protected by three meningeal layers; from outermost to innermost these are:
o: Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Dura is outermost, pia is innermost, directly adherent to neural tissue.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Cerebrospinal fluid is located within the:
o: Subarachnoid space, between arachnoid and pia mater
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: CSF fills the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The epidural space, used clinically for epidural anesthesia, is located:
o: Between pia mater and spinal cord
Between the dura mater and the vertebral canal wall (periosteum/ligamentum flavum)
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The epidural space lies outside the dura, within the bony vertebral canal.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: In cross-section, the spinal cord's gray matter is centrally located and organized into:
o: A single undifferentiated mass with no functional divisions
White matter surrounding a hollow core with no gray matter
Dorsal (posterior) horns primarily sensory and ventral (anterior) horns primarily motor
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Dorsal horns process sensory input; ventral horns house motor neurons.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The corticospinal tract, the major descending motor pathway, is located in which region of spinal cord white matter?
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The lateral corticospinal tract descends in the lateral white matter column.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) primarily carry which sensory modality?
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Dorsal columns carry discriminative touch, vibration, and joint position sense.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The spinothalamic tract primarily carries which sensory modalities?
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The spinothalamic tract is the principal pathway for pain and temperature.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: A lesion of the dorsal columns would most likely impair:
o: Proprioception and vibration sense, with relatively preserved pain/temperature
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Dorsal column lesions selectively impair proprioception/vibration, sparing pain/temperature pathways.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The dorsal root of a spinal nerve carries primarily:
o: Sensory (afferent) fibers, with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion
No fibers, purely a structural component
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The dorsal root carries sensory input into the spinal cord.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The ventral root of a spinal nerve carries primarily:
o: Motor (efferent) fibers to muscles and autonomic targets
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The ventral root carries motor output from the spinal cord.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Erector spinae muscles, running longitudinally along the vertebral column, primarily function to:
o: Extend the vertebral column and maintain posture
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Erector spinae is the chief extensor group of the vertebral column.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The trapezius muscle, a superficial back muscle, is innervated by the:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Trapezius is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The latissimus dorsi muscle's primary actions include extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Latissimus dorsi is a powerful shoulder extensor/adductor/medial rotator.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Spina bifida occulta, a common minor vertebral defect, involves:
o: A tumor of the spinal cord
Complete exposure of the spinal cord
Failure of fusion of the vertebral arch (lamina) without herniation of neural tissue
Absence of the entire vertebral column
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Occulta is a mild, usually asymptomatic failure of posterior arch fusion, covered by skin.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Scoliosis refers to an abnormal:
o: Rotation of a single vertebra without curvature
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Scoliosis is defined by an abnormal lateral spinal curvature, often with rotation.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Kyphosis refers to an exaggerated:
o: Anterior curvature of the lumbar spine
Posterior (convex) curvature of the thoracic spine
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Kyphosis is an exaggerated thoracic posterior convexity.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Lordosis refers to an exaggerated:
o: Anterior (concave) curvature, normally present in the cervical and lumbar spine
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Lordosis is an exaggerated anterior concavity, normally seen in cervical/lumbar regions.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The sacroiliac joint connects the sacrum to the:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The sacroiliac joint links the sacrum to the ilium, transmitting weight to the lower limbs.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The spinal nerve exiting between C7 and T1 is typically named:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: C8 exits below C7 since there are 8 cervical nerves but only 7 cervical vertebrae.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Unlike other spinal levels, cervical spinal nerves C1-C7 exit:
o: They do not exit through foramina
Only at the level of C1
Above their corresponding vertebra (C8 exits below C7, and thereafter nerves exit below their same-numbered vertebra)
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Cervical nerves C1-C7 exit above their same-numbered vertebra; below C7 the pattern shifts.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Referred pain from the diaphragm (innervated by C3-C5, phrenic nerve) is classically felt at the:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Shared C3-C5 dermatomal origin explains diaphragmatic pain referred to the shoulder tip.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: A 'dermatome' is defined as:
o: A muscle group sharing one nerve
An area of skin innervated by sensory fibers from a single spinal nerve root
A region supplied by one artery
An area of skin supplied by a single muscle
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Dermatomes map cutaneous sensory territory to specific spinal nerve roots.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: A 'myotome' refers to:
o: A skin area supplied by one nerve root
The group of muscles innervated by a single spinal nerve root
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Myotomes describe muscle innervation by spinal nerve root, analogous to dermatomes for skin.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of nerve roots below the level of the:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Below the conus medullaris, the canal contains only the cauda equina nerve roots.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The vertebral artery ascends through the transverse foramina of which vertebrae before entering the skull?
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: The vertebral artery travels through cervical transverse foramina en route to the skull.

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.s: The spinal cord shows two enlargements corresponding to limb innervation; these are the cervical and:
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.e: Cervical and lumbosacral enlargements reflect the greater neural supply needed for the limbs.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Endochondral ossification, the process forming most long bones, begins with a template of:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: A hyaline cartilage model is progressively replaced by bone in endochondral ossification.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Intramembranous ossification, forming flat bones like the skull, occurs directly within:
o: Mesenchymal (fibrous) connective tissue, without a cartilage intermediate
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Flat bones ossify directly from condensed mesenchyme, skipping a cartilage stage.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: The epiphyseal (growth) plate is composed of:
o: Hyaline cartilage, allowing longitudinal bone growth until fusion
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: The growth plate is hyaline cartilage that ossifies progressively until closure at maturity.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: The zone of the epiphyseal plate closest to the epiphysis, containing resting chondrocytes, is the:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: The resting zone anchors the plate and provides a chondrocyte reserve.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Longitudinal bone growth results primarily from chondrocyte proliferation in the:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Active chondrocyte division in the proliferative zone drives lengthening.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Bone remodeling is a coordinated process involving:
o: A process that stops completely after skeletal maturity
Coupled activity of osteoclasts (resorption) and osteoblasts (formation)
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Remodeling continues throughout life via coordinated resorption and formation.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises serum calcium primarily by:
o: Stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and activation of vitamin D
Decreasing renal phosphate reabsorption exclusively with no other effects
Directly increasing intestinal calcium absorption without vitamin D
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: PTH acts on bone, kidney, and indirectly on the gut (via vitamin D activation) to raise calcium.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Calcitonin, secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, functions to:
o: Increase renal calcium excretion by direct tubular action only
Lower serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Calcitonin opposes PTH by inhibiting osteoclasts, lowering serum calcium.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Active vitamin D (calcitriol) increases serum calcium primarily by:
o: Increasing intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Calcitriol's principal action is enhancing gut absorption of calcium and phosphate.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Osteomalacia/rickets classically results from deficiency of:
o: Vitamin D (impaired mineralization of bone matrix)
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Vitamin D deficiency impairs mineralization, causing soft, weak bone.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Osteoporosis is characterized by:
o: Reduced bone mass/density with normal mineralization ratio, increasing fracture risk
Increased bone formation exceeding resorption chronically
Normal bone mineral density with abnormal shape
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Osteoporosis reflects reduced bone quantity, normally mineralized, raising fracture risk.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Synovial joints are characterized by the presence of a:
o: Joint cavity containing synovial fluid, lined by synovial membrane
Fibrous joint capsule without a cavity
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: A synovial-fluid-filled cavity distinguishes synovial joints from fibrous/cartilaginous joints.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Synovial fluid's primary functions include lubrication and:
o: Generating electrical signals for proprioception exclusively
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Since articular cartilage lacks blood vessels, synovial fluid supplies its nutrition.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Hyaluronic acid, a major component of synovial fluid, is secreted by:
o: Synoviocytes (type B) of the synovial membrane
Fibroblasts of the joint capsule exclusively
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Type B synoviocytes secrete hyaluronan, giving synovial fluid its viscosity.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Articular (hyaline) cartilage lacks which structure, limiting its capacity for repair?
o: Blood vessels, nerves, and a perichondrium
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Being avascular and aneural with no perichondrium limits articular cartilage's healing ability.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Osteoarthritis is characterized primarily by:
o: Progressive degeneration of articular cartilage with subchondral bone changes, typically age/wear-related
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: OA is a degenerative 'wear and tear' joint disease, not primarily autoimmune.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Rheumatoid arthritis, unlike osteoarthritis, is primarily characterized by:
o: An autoimmune inflammatory process affecting the synovium, often symmetric and involving small joints
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: RA is an autoimmune synovitis, classically symmetric and affecting small joints.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Synovial joints are functionally classified based on the number of axes of movement; a hinge joint allows movement in:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Hinge joints like the elbow allow motion in a single plane.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: A ball-and-socket joint is classified functionally as:
o: Multiaxial (triaxial), allowing the greatest range of motion
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Ball-and-socket joints allow the widest range of movement in multiple planes.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Fibrous joints, such as sutures of the skull, typically allow:
o: The same range of motion as synovial joints
Movement in a single plane freely
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Fibrous joints are generally immobile, providing stability.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Cartilaginous joints, such as the pubic symphysis, generally allow:
o: Full range of motion like synovial joints
They are not a joint category
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Cartilaginous joints allow limited, slight movement.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Osteocytes reside within small spaces in bone matrix called:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Lacunae house individual osteocytes within mineralized bone matrix.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Canaliculi in bone tissue primarily function to:
o: Connect osteocytes to each other and to blood supply via cytoplasmic processes for nutrient exchange
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Canaliculi are tiny channels allowing osteocyte processes to communicate and exchange nutrients.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Volkmann's canals in compact bone function to:
o: Connect Haversian canals to each other and to the periosteal/endosteal surface, carrying blood vessels transversely
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Volkmann's (perforating) canals run transversely, linking osteons' vascular supply.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Trabecular (spongy/cancellous) bone, compared to compact bone, has:
o: A honeycomb-like network of trabeculae with marrow spaces, providing strength with less weight
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Trabecular bone's porous architecture balances strength and lightness, and is metabolically active.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Woven bone is remodeled into mature lamellar bone during:
o: Fetal life exclusively, with no postnatal remodeling
Normal bone development, growth, and fracture healing throughout life
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Woven bone is a normal transitional stage, remodeled into organized lamellar bone.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Wolff's law describes how bone:
o: Only responds to hormonal signals, not mechanical stress
Remodels and adapts its structure in response to mechanical loading/stress
Always maintains constant density regardless of loading
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Bone architecture adapts to the mechanical demands placed upon it.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: A fracture healing sequence typically proceeds through hematoma formation, soft callus, hard (bony) callus, and:
o: Bone remodeling, restoring the original shape over time
Immediate return to normal architecture with no remodeling
No further changes after hard callus
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Remodeling is the final stage, sculpting the healed bone back toward its original form.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Osteoclasts resorb bone by secreting:
o: Hydrogen ions and proteolytic enzymes (e.g., cathepsin K) to dissolve mineral and matrix
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Osteoclasts acidify and enzymatically digest bone matrix to resorb it.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme marker of osteoblast activity, functions in bone mineralization by:
o: Hydrolyzing phosphate esters, raising local phosphate concentration to promote hydroxyapatite crystal formation
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Alkaline phosphatase generates free phosphate locally to drive mineral crystal formation.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Hydroxyapatite, the principal mineral component of bone, is primarily composed of:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Hydroxyapatite is a crystalline calcium phosphate salt.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Type I collagen is the predominant organic matrix protein in:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Type I collagen provides tensile strength to bone, tendon, and ligament matrix.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Type II collagen is the predominant collagen type in:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Type II collagen is characteristic of cartilage matrix.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Proteoglycans in cartilage matrix function primarily to:
o: Attract and retain water, giving cartilage its compressive resilience
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Proteoglycans' negative charge attracts water, allowing cartilage to resist compression.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Achondroplasia, a common cause of dwarfism, results from a defect affecting:
o: Collagen type I in bone matrix only
Endochondral ossification (cartilage proliferation at growth plates) due to FGFR3 mutation
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: FGFR3 mutations impair growth plate cartilage proliferation, shortening long bones.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Osteogenesis imperfecta ('brittle bone disease') most commonly results from a defect in:
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Mutations affecting type I collagen weaken bone, causing fragility fractures.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Paget's disease of bone is characterized by:
o: Disorganized, excessive bone remodeling, producing structurally weak, enlarged bone
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Paget's disease features chaotic, accelerated remodeling, weakening affected bone.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Sesamoid bones, such as the patella, develop within:
o: Tendons, where they reduce friction and alter the angle of pull
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Sesamoid bones form within tendons, improving mechanical advantage.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: The periosteum, the connective tissue covering the outer surface of bone, contributes to:
o: Bone's blood supply, nerve supply, and appositional (width) growth
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: The periosteum supplies vessels/nerves and houses osteoprogenitor cells for width growth.

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.s: Bursae, fluid-filled sacs near joints, primarily function to:
o: Reduce friction between tendons, muscles, and bones during movement
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.e: Bursae cushion and reduce friction at points of mechanical stress near joints.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: The functional contractile unit of skeletal muscle is the:
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: The sarcomere, bounded by Z-lines, is the basic repeating contractile unit.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: During muscle contraction, the sliding filament theory describes:
o: No movement of filaments, only chemical change
Shortening of the actin and myosin filaments themselves
Actin filaments sliding past myosin filaments without either filament shortening
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Filament lengths stay constant; sarcomere shortening comes from filaments sliding over each other.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: The A band of the sarcomere corresponds to:
o: The length of the myosin (thick) filaments, which remains constant during contraction
Actin filaments only, changing length during contraction
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: The A band marks the full length of thick filaments and stays constant.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: The I band of the sarcomere, containing only thin (actin) filaments, does what during contraction?
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: As filaments overlap more during contraction, the I band narrows.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Calcium ions trigger muscle contraction by binding to:
o: Troponin C, causing a conformational shift that moves tropomyosin off the actin binding site
Myosin heads directly to activate ATPase
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Calcium binding troponin C exposes the myosin-binding site on actin.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Calcium for skeletal muscle contraction is released from the:
o: Sarcoplasmic reticulum, triggered by depolarization via T-tubules
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: T-tubule depolarization triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: The neuromuscular junction releases which neurotransmitter to trigger muscle fiber depolarization?
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the skeletal neuromuscular junction.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction functions to:
o: Degrade acetylcholine, terminating its action and allowing muscle relaxation
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Acetylcholinesterase rapidly breaks down ACh, ending the signal at the synapse.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Myasthenia gravis results from autoantibodies against:
o: Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Autoantibodies against nicotinic ACh receptors impair neuromuscular transmission.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Rigor mortis, the stiffening of muscles after death, occurs because:
o: Calcium is completely removed from muscle
ATP depletion prevents myosin heads from detaching from actin, locking the cross-bridge
