musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Without ATP, myosin cannot release actin, locking muscle in a contracted state.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Skeletal muscle fibers are classified as type I (slow-twitch, oxidative) or type II (fast-twitch, glycolytic); type I fibers are best suited for:
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Type I fibers rely on oxidative metabolism, favoring endurance over power.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Type IIb (fast glycolytic) muscle fibers are characterized by:
o: Rapid, powerful contraction relying on anaerobic glycolysis, fatiguing quickly
High mitochondrial content and fatigue resistance
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Type IIb fibers generate rapid force via anaerobic pathways but fatigue quickly.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: A motor unit is defined as:
o: A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: A motor unit comprises one motor neuron plus every fiber it controls.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Muscles requiring fine motor control (e.g., extraocular muscles) typically have:
o: Small motor units, with few muscle fibers per motor neuron
Large motor units with many fibers per neuron
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Small motor units allow finer gradations of force and control.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Muscle fatigue during sustained exercise is associated with factors including:
o: Depletion of energy substrates, accumulation of metabolites (e.g., lactate, H+), and impaired calcium handling
Complete depletion of calcium stores with no other cause
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Fatigue is multifactorial, involving substrate depletion and metabolite accumulation.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: During short, intense exercise, skeletal muscle relies most heavily on:
o: The phosphocreatine system and anaerobic glycolysis
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Rapid ATP needs during short bursts are met by phosphocreatine and glycolysis.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Phosphocreatine (creatine phosphate) in muscle functions as a:
o: Rapidly mobilizable high-energy phosphate reserve to regenerate ATP
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Phosphocreatine quickly donates its phosphate to regenerate ATP from ADP.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Myoglobin in muscle tissue functions primarily to:
o: Store oxygen within muscle fibers for use during contraction
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Myoglobin is an intracellular oxygen store, buffering supply during activity.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Smooth muscle contraction, unlike skeletal muscle, relies on calcium binding to:
o: Calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase
Actin directly without any regulatory protein
Tropomyosin directly without any calcium-binding protein
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Smooth muscle lacks troponin, instead using the calcium-calmodulin-MLCK pathway.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Smooth muscle lacks troponin but is regulated instead by the:
o: Calcium-calmodulin-myosin light chain kinase pathway, phosphorylating myosin light chains
T-tubule system identical to skeletal muscle
Sarcomere structure identical to skeletal muscle
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Phosphorylation of myosin light chains, via calmodulin-activated MLCK, enables smooth muscle contraction.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Cardiac muscle differs from skeletal muscle in that cardiac muscle:
o: Has intercalated discs allowing electrical coupling and functions as a functional syncytium
Has multiple peripheral nuclei per cell
Cannot generate its own action potentials
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Intercalated discs electrically couple cardiac cells, allowing coordinated contraction as a syncytium.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Isotonic muscle contraction refers to contraction in which:
o: Muscle length stays constant while tension changes
Muscle tension remains relatively constant while muscle length changes (shortening or lengthening)
No movement or tension change occurs
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Isotonic contractions maintain roughly constant tension while the muscle changes length.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Isometric muscle contraction refers to contraction in which:
o: Muscle tension increases without a significant change in muscle length (e.g., pushing against an immovable object)
The muscle shortens against a constant load
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Isometric contractions generate force without appreciable muscle shortening.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: An eccentric muscle contraction occurs when:
o: No force is generated at all
The muscle lengthens while still generating force (e.g., lowering a weight in a controlled manner)
The muscle shortens while generating force
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Eccentric contraction controls lengthening of an active muscle under load.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: The 'all-or-none' principle in skeletal muscle physiology applies to:
o: A single muscle fiber's response to an adequate stimulus (it either fully contracts or does not contract at all)
The entire motor unit pool regardless of stimulus strength
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: A single fiber's contraction is all-or-none once threshold is reached, though whole-muscle force is graded.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Muscle tension can be graded (varied) in the whole muscle primarily through:
o: Changing the all-or-none threshold of a single fiber
Recruitment of additional motor units and varying firing frequency (summation)
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Whole-muscle force is graded via motor unit recruitment and frequency of stimulation.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Tetanus (sustained maximal contraction) in skeletal muscle results from:
o: High-frequency stimulation causing summation of twitches without full relaxation between stimuli
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Rapid successive stimuli prevent relaxation between twitches, producing sustained tetanic tension.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Denervated skeletal muscle typically undergoes:
o: Atrophy, due to loss of neural trophic influence and disuse
Conversion entirely to type I fibers
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Loss of innervation leads to progressive muscle wasting (atrophy).

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from a mutation in the gene encoding:
o: Dystrophin, a protein stabilizing the muscle cell membrane during contraction
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Absent dystrophin destabilizes the sarcolemma, leading to progressive muscle degeneration.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Creatine kinase (CK), often elevated in blood after muscle injury, functions physiologically to:
o: Catalyze transfer of a phosphate group between creatine phosphate and ADP to regenerate ATP
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: CK regenerates ATP from phosphocreatine and ADP during rapid energy demand.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Calcium homeostasis in the body is tightly regulated because calcium is essential for:
o: Muscle contraction, nerve conduction, blood clotting, and enzyme activity, among other roles
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Calcium is a multifunctional ion critical to numerous physiological processes.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Approximately what percentage of total body calcium is stored in bone?
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Roughly 99% of body calcium resides in the skeleton as hydroxyapatite.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Hypocalcemia can cause increased neuromuscular excitability, manifesting as:
o: Tetany (muscle twitching/spasm, e.g., Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs)
Bradycardia exclusively with no muscular signs
Muscle weakness and flaccid paralysis only
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Low calcium lowers the threshold for nerve/muscle depolarization, causing tetany.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Hypercalcemia classically produces symptoms remembered by the mnemonic 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones,' reflecting effects including:
o: Decreased neuromuscular excitability, renal stones, bone pain, and GI/psychiatric symptoms
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: High calcium reduces neuromuscular excitability and affects kidneys, bones, gut, and mood.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Phosphate is important in bone biochemistry as a component of:
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Phosphate combines with calcium to form the hydroxyapatite mineral of bone.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Osteocalcin, a protein produced by osteoblasts, is used clinically as a marker of:
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Osteocalcin is a specific product of active osteoblasts, reflecting bone formation.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Collagen cross-linking, important for tensile strength in bone and connective tissue, depends on the enzyme:
o: Hydroxylase acting alone without lysyl oxidase
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Lysyl oxidase catalyzes cross-link formation between collagen molecules.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Vitamin D deficiency in growing children classically produces:
o: Rickets, with bowing of long bones due to poor mineralization
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: In children with open growth plates, vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Gout results from deposition of which crystals in joints?
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition from hyperuricemia.

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.s: Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease) is distinguished from gout by the type of crystal and its characteristic:
o: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals (gout) versus rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals (pseudogout) under polarized light
musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.e: Polarized light microscopy distinguishes urate (negative birefringence) from CPPD (weak positive birefringence) crystals.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The heart is located in which compartment of the thorax?
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The heart and pericardium occupy the middle mediastinum.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The pericardium consists of an outer fibrous layer and an inner serous layer; the serous pericardium itself has:
o: Parietal and visceral (epicardial) layers, with pericardial fluid between them
No relationship to the heart wall
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The serous pericardium's two layers enclose a fluid-filled space allowing frictionless movement.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Cardiac tamponade results from:
o: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, compressing the heart
Excess air in the pleural space
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Pericardial fluid accumulation restricts cardiac filling, impairing output.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The right atrium receives venous blood from the:
o: Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and coronary sinus
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Systemic venous return and coronary venous drainage enter the right atrium.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The right ventricle ejects blood into the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The four pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The left ventricle, with the thickest myocardial wall, ejects blood into the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation via the aorta.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The tricuspid valve is located between the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The tricuspid valve is the right-sided atrioventricular valve.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The mitral (bicuspid) valve is located between the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The mitral valve is the left-sided atrioventricular valve.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The pulmonary valve is located between the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The pulmonary semilunar valve guards the right ventricular outflow tract.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The aortic valve is located between the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The aortic semilunar valve guards the left ventricular outflow tract.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Papillary muscles and chordae tendineae function together to:
o: Prevent prolapse of the atrioventricular valves into the atria during ventricular systole
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: This apparatus anchors AV valve leaflets, preventing backward billowing during systole.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The right coronary artery typically supplies the:
o: Right atrium, right ventricle, and (in most people) the SA and AV nodes
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The RCA supplies the right heart and, in most people, the conduction system nodes.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The left anterior descending (LAD) artery, a branch of the left coronary artery, primarily supplies the:
o: Anterior interventricular septum and anterior wall of the left ventricle
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The LAD is the key vessel for the anterior septum and left ventricular wall.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The circumflex artery, a branch of the left coronary artery, primarily supplies the:
o: Lateral and posterior walls of the left ventricle
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The circumflex artery runs in the atrioventricular groove, supplying lateral/posterior LV.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Coronary sinus blood drains into the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Most cardiac venous blood collects in the coronary sinus, emptying into the right atrium.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The interventricular septum separates the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The interventricular septum divides the right and left ventricles.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The fossa ovalis, a depression on the interatrial septum, represents the remnant of the fetal:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: After birth, the foramen ovale closes, leaving the fossa ovalis depression.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Auscultation of the mitral valve is best performed at the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The cardiac apex is the classic auscultation point for mitral valve sounds.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Auscultation of the aortic valve is best performed at the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The aortic area is the right second intercostal space near the sternum.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The heart's apex is normally located at approximately:
o: The left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The apex beat is classically palpated at the left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The pericardiacophrenic vessels travel with which nerve, which also supplies sensory innervation to the pericardium?
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The phrenic nerve accompanies the pericardiacophrenic vessels and supplies pericardial sensation.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The heart receives parasympathetic innervation via the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Vagal fibers provide parasympathetic input, mainly to the SA/AV nodes.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Sympathetic innervation of the heart primarily increases:
o: Only vascular resistance, without cardiac effects
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Cardiac sympathetic fibers boost rate and contractile force.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation of the heart primarily:
o: Has no effect on the heart
Decreases heart rate, mainly acting on the SA and AV nodes
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Vagal tone slows the SA node and delays AV conduction.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The pericardial cavity normally contains a small amount of fluid, functioning to:
o: Reduce friction between the visceral and parietal pericardial layers during heartbeats
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: A thin fluid film lubricates the pericardial surfaces during cardiac motion.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The great cardiac vein runs alongside which coronary artery?
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The great cardiac vein accompanies the LAD before draining into the coronary sinus.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The atrioventricular (AV) fibrous rings function to:
o: Provide structural support for valve attachment and electrically insulate atria from ventricles (except through the AV node)
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The fibrous skeleton anchors valves and isolates atrial from ventricular myocardium electrically.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The pectinate muscles are ridge-like structures found in the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Pectinate muscles line the atrial appendages, giving a ridged appearance.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges found in the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Trabeculae carneae line the internal ventricular walls.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula), found in the right ventricle, carries part of the:
o: Right bundle branch, helping coordinate right ventricular contraction
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The moderator band conducts part of the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The heart develops embryologically from the:
o: Primary heart tube, formed from splanchnic mesoderm
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Cardiac progenitor cells in splanchnic mesoderm form the primitive heart tube.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Congenital patent ductus arteriosus results from failure of closure of the fetal connection between the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The ductus arteriosus normally connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta in fetal life.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: An atrial septal defect involves an abnormal opening between the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: ASD is a persistent communication between the left and right atria.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: A ventricular septal defect, the most common congenital heart defect, involves an abnormal opening between the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: VSD is an opening in the interventricular septum, the most common congenital cardiac anomaly.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Tetralogy of Fallot classically includes four features: ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy, and:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Pulmonary stenosis is the fourth classic component of tetralogy of Fallot.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: Coarctation of the aorta most commonly occurs:
o: Near the ligamentum arteriosum, distal to the left subclavian artery
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: Juxtaductal coarctation near the ligamentum arteriosum is the classic location.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The azygos vein system primarily drains blood from the:
o: Posterior thoracic and abdominal wall into the superior vena cava
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The azygos system drains the posterior body wall, emptying into the SVC.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The mediastinum is divided into superior and inferior compartments; the inferior mediastinum is further divided into anterior, middle, and:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The inferior mediastinum comprises anterior, middle, and posterior subdivisions.

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.s: The heart's base (posterior surface), formed mainly by the left atrium, faces the:
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.e: The heart's base lies posteriorly, adjacent to the esophagus and descending aorta.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The cardiac cycle is divided into two main phases:
o: Contraction and relaxation only, without further subdivision
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Systole and diastole are the two fundamental phases of the cardiac cycle.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Isovolumetric contraction occurs when:
o: Only the AV valves are open
All four heart valves are closed while ventricular pressure rises before ejection
Both AV and semilunar valves are open
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Pressure builds with all valves shut until it exceeds arterial pressure, opening semilunar valves.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Ventricular ejection begins when:
o: Ventricular pressure exceeds arterial (aortic/pulmonary) pressure, opening the semilunar valves
The QRS complex ends, unrelated to pressure
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Once ventricular pressure surpasses arterial pressure, the semilunar valves open and ejection begins.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by:
o: Closure of the AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the start of systole
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: S1 marks AV valve closure at the onset of ventricular systole.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The second heart sound (S2) is produced by:
o: Closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves at the start of diastole
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: S2 marks semilunar valve closure at the onset of diastole.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Cardiac output is calculated as:
o: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
Blood pressure multiplied by heart rate
Heart rate divided by stroke volume
Mean arterial pressure divided by total peripheral resistance
Stroke volume divided by ejection fraction
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Stroke volume is defined as:
o: Heart rate multiplied by cardiac output
Total blood volume in the body
Cardiac output divided by body surface area
The volume of blood ejected by a ventricle per beat (end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume)
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Stroke volume is EDV minus ESV for a single beat.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: According to the Frank-Starling law of the heart, increased venous return (preload) leads to:
o: Increased stretch of cardiac muscle fibers, producing increased force of contraction and stroke volume (within physiological limits)
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Greater myocardial stretch increases contractile force up to a physiological limit.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Afterload refers to:
o: The resistance/pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject blood
The volume of blood filling the ventricle before contraction
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must generate to open the semilunar valve and eject blood.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Increased afterload (e.g., hypertension) tends to:
o: Have no effect on the heart
Decrease stroke volume for a given contractility, if uncompensated
Increase stroke volume for a given contractility
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Higher afterload makes ejection harder, reducing stroke volume unless compensated.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Ejection fraction is defined as:
o: End-systolic volume divided by end-diastolic volume
Mean arterial pressure divided by cardiac output
Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, expressed as a percentage
Cardiac output divided by heart rate
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: EF = SV/EDV x 100%, a key index of systolic function.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: A normal resting ejection fraction is approximately:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Normal EF at rest is roughly 55-70%.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Sympathetic stimulation increases myocardial contractility primarily via which receptor?
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Beta-1 receptors mediate sympathetic effects on heart rate and contractility.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Parasympathetic stimulation slows the heart rate primarily via which receptor on the SA node?
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Vagal acetylcholine acts on M2 muscarinic receptors to slow the SA node.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The SA node normally has the fastest intrinsic rate of depolarization, making it the:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: The SA node's fastest intrinsic rate makes it the heart's normal pacemaker.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: If the SA node fails, which structure typically takes over as a backup pacemaker, at a slower intrinsic rate?
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: The AV node has the next-highest intrinsic rate and serves as backup pacemaker.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Venous return to the heart is enhanced by which mechanisms?
o: The skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pump, and venous valves
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Muscle contraction and respiratory pressure changes, aided by valves, promote venous return.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Central venous pressure primarily reflects:
o: Right atrial pressure, related to venous return and right heart function
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: CVP approximates right atrial pressure, a proxy for venous return/right heart status.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricle occurs predominantly during:
o: Diastole, when myocardial compression of vessels is minimal
Equally throughout the cardiac cycle with no variation
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: LV myocardial compression during systole limits flow, so most perfusion occurs in diastole.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The heart's primary metabolic fuel under normal aerobic conditions is:
o: Fatty acids (predominantly), with glucose and lactate as additional substrates
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: The heart preferentially oxidizes fatty acids, supplemented by glucose/lactate.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Cardiac muscle has an abundance of mitochondria because it:
o: Relies heavily on continuous aerobic (oxidative) metabolism for ATP production
Stores large amounts of glycogen instead of using mitochondria
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Continuous contraction demands sustained oxidative ATP production.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The a wave of the jugular venous pulse corresponds to:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: The a wave reflects right atrial contraction against the tricuspid valve.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Baroreceptors located in the carotid sinus and aortic arch primarily respond to:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors sensing arterial pressure changes.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: An increase in arterial pressure sensed by baroreceptors leads to:
o: Increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic output, raising heart rate
Increased parasympathetic and decreased sympathetic output, lowering heart rate and blood pressure
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Rising pressure triggers a reflex that lowers heart rate/pressure back toward baseline.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Preload is best approximated clinically by:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Preload reflects the degree of ventricular filling/stretch before contraction.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The Bainbridge reflex describes how increased venous return/atrial stretch leads to:
o: Increased heart rate via stretch receptors in the atria
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Atrial stretch receptors trigger a reflex tachycardia, matching output to increased filling.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Positive inotropic agents primarily act to:
o: Increase the force/strength of myocardial contraction
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Inotropy refers to contractile force; positive inotropes enhance it.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: A positive chronotropic effect refers to:
o: Increased stroke volume without rate change
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Chronotropy pertains to heart rate; positive chronotropes increase it.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: A positive dromotropic effect refers to:
o: Increased conduction velocity, particularly through the AV node
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Dromotropy pertains to conduction velocity, especially through the AV node.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Total peripheral resistance is most influenced by the diameter of the:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Arterioles, as the main resistance vessels, chiefly determine TPR.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) can be approximated as:
o: Diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure
Average of systolic and diastolic pressure exactly (in all cases)
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: MAP is commonly approximated as DBP + 1/3(pulse pressure).

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Pulse pressure is defined as the difference between:
o: Mean arterial pressure and diastolic pressure
Central venous pressure and arterial pressure
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Pulse pressure = systolic BP minus diastolic BP.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The dicrotic notch seen on an arterial pressure waveform corresponds to:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: The dicrotic notch reflects the brief backflow closing the aortic valve.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Cardiac reserve refers to the heart's ability to:
o: Increase cardiac output above resting levels to meet increased metabolic demand (e.g., during exercise)
Maintain a fixed cardiac output regardless of demand
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Cardiac reserve is the capacity to raise output well above resting levels when needed.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: During moderate dynamic exercise, cardiac output increases primarily due to:
o: No change, as cardiac output is fixed
Decreased heart rate and increased stroke volume only
Increased heart rate and increased stroke volume (via increased venous return and contractility)
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Both heart rate and stroke volume rise during moderate exercise to boost output.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Starling's law of the capillaries governs:
o: Fluid movement between capillaries and interstitial space, based on hydrostatic and oncotic pressures
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Starling forces determine net filtration or reabsorption across capillary walls.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure favors:
o: Fluid filtration out of capillaries into the interstitium, potentially causing edema
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Higher hydrostatic pressure pushes more fluid out of the capillary into tissue.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., in hypoalbuminemia) favors:
o: Fluid filtration out into tissues, contributing to edema
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Low plasma protein reduces the pull retaining fluid in vessels, favoring interstitial edema.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: The Valsalva maneuver (forced exhalation against a closed glottis) causes an initial:
o: Increase in venous return and cardiac output
Decrease in venous return due to increased intrathoracic pressure, transiently lowering cardiac output and blood pressure
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Raised intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return, initially dropping cardiac output/pressure.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.s: Cardiogenic shock results from:
o: Severe impairment of the heart's pumping ability, leading to inadequate tissue perfusion
Spinal cord injury causing loss of sympathetic tone
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.e: Cardiogenic shock arises from primary pump failure, not volume loss or vasodilation.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The P wave on an ECG represents:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The P wave reflects the spread of depolarization across the atria.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The QRS complex on an ECG represents:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The QRS complex reflects ventricular depolarization.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The T wave on an ECG represents:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The T wave reflects ventricular repolarization.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The PR interval represents the time from:
o: Onset of ventricular depolarization to its end
Onset of atrial depolarization to the onset of ventricular depolarization (reflecting AV nodal delay)
End of the QRS to the T wave
Onset of the T wave to its end
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: PR interval spans atrial depolarization onset to ventricular depolarization onset.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: A prolonged PR interval (greater than 200 ms) is characteristic of:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: First-degree AV block is defined by a fixed, prolonged PR interval.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The QT interval represents:
o: The total duration of ventricular depolarization and repolarization
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: QT interval spans the entire ventricular electrical cycle, depolarization through repolarization.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The ST segment on an ECG normally represents:
o: The period between ventricular depolarization and repolarization (plateau phase), normally isoelectric
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The ST segment corresponds to the plateau phase, normally at baseline.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: ST segment elevation on an ECG is classically associated with:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: ST elevation is the hallmark of acute STEMI.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The cardiac action potential in ventricular myocytes has a prolonged plateau phase (phase 2) due to:
o: Calcium influx through L-type calcium channels balanced by potassium efflux
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Balanced calcium influx and potassium efflux sustain the characteristic plateau.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Phase 0 (rapid depolarization) of the ventricular cardiac action potential is due to:
o: Rapid sodium influx through fast sodium channels
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Fast sodium channel opening drives the rapid upstroke of phase 0.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Phase 4 of the SA node's pacemaker action potential, responsible for spontaneous depolarization, is largely due to:
o: The 'funny current' (If), a slow inward sodium/potassium current
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The funny current drives slow spontaneous depolarization in pacemaker cells.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The AV node normally provides a delay in impulse conduction, which functions to:
o: Allow the atria to complete contraction and empty into the ventricles before ventricular contraction begins
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: AV nodal delay coordinates sequential atrial then ventricular contraction.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The bundle of His and Purkinje fibers function to:
o: Delay conduction between atria and ventricles
Rapidly conduct the electrical impulse throughout the ventricles for coordinated contraction
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: This system rapidly distributes the impulse for synchronized ventricular contraction.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Lead II of a standard 12-lead ECG records the electrical potential difference between:
o: The right arm and left arm
The right leg and left leg
The right arm and left leg
The left arm and left leg
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Lead II records between the right arm and left leg, roughly parallel to the heart's electrical axis.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Atrial fibrillation on ECG is characterized by:
o: Absence of discrete P waves, with an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm
Regular P waves before each QRS
A prolonged PR interval with normal rhythm
A widened QRS with regular rhythm
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Chaotic atrial activity replaces organized P waves, producing an irregularly irregular rhythm.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Ventricular fibrillation is a life-threatening arrhythmia characterized by:
o: Chaotic, disorganized electrical activity with no effective ventricular contraction, requiring immediate defibrillation
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: VF is a medical emergency with no effective cardiac output, requiring defibrillation.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Third-degree (complete) AV block is characterized by:
o: A fixed prolonged PR interval with every QRS conducted
Complete dissociation between atrial (P wave) and ventricular (QRS) activity
Progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: In complete heart block, atria and ventricles beat independently.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The refractory period of cardiac muscle, which is relatively long compared to skeletal muscle, functions to:
o: Prevent tetanic contraction, ensuring the heart has time to fill and eject blood rhythmically
Allow tetanic contraction of the heart
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: A long refractory period protects the heart from tetany, which would prevent filling.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: An ectopic pacemaker refers to:
o: The AV node functioning normally as backup
An abnormal site outside the SA node initiating the heartbeat
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: An ectopic focus is any site other than the SA node that initiates a beat abnormally.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Hyperkalemia's classic early ECG change is:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Early hyperkalemia classically produces tall, peaked T waves.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Severe hyperkalemia can progress to ECG changes including:
o: Isolated P wave changes with no other effect
Shortening of the PR interval only
Widening of the QRS complex and eventual sine-wave pattern, risking cardiac arrest
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Severe hyperkalemia widens the QRS and can progress to a sine-wave pattern preceding arrest.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Hypokalemia's classic ECG findings include:
o: Peaked T waves and shortened QT
Flattened T waves, U waves, and prolonged QT interval
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Hypokalemia classically flattens T waves, produces U waves, and prolongs QT.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Hypercalcemia classically shortens the:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Hypercalcemia shortens the QT interval by shortening the plateau phase.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Hypocalcemia classically causes:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Hypocalcemia prolongs the QT interval, raising arrhythmia risk.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: A delta wave on ECG, with a short PR interval, is characteristic of:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: An accessory pathway pre-excites the ventricle, producing a delta wave and short PR.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Sinus tachycardia is defined as a heart rate above approximately:
o: It is not a rate-based definition
100 bpm, originating normally from the SA node
150 bpm exclusively from the AV node
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Sinus tachycardia is SA-node-origin rhythm faster than about 100 bpm.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Sinus bradycardia is defined as a heart rate below approximately:
o: It cannot be diagnosed by rate alone
60 bpm, with normal SA node origin
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Sinus bradycardia is a normally-originating rhythm slower than about 60 bpm.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The absolute refractory period of cardiac muscle corresponds roughly to the duration of the:
o: QRS complex through most of the T wave (the plateau phase of the action potential)
ST segment exclusively, without the QRS
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The long plateau phase underlies cardiac muscle's extended absolute refractory period.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Automaticity, the ability of certain cardiac cells to spontaneously depolarize, is a property most prominent in:
o: Purkinje fibers exclusively, with no automaticity elsewhere
Pacemaker cells such as those of the SA and AV nodes
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Pacemaker cells (SA/AV nodes, and to a lesser extent Purkinje fibers) show automaticity.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Digoxin, used in heart failure and atrial fibrillation, works partly by increasing vagal tone, which:
o: Slows AV nodal conduction, helping control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Enhanced vagal tone from digoxin slows AV conduction, controlling ventricular response rate.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Class I antiarrhythmic drugs primarily act by blocking:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Class I agents block fast sodium channels, slowing conduction.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Beta-blockers (Class II antiarrhythmics) reduce arrhythmia risk primarily by:
o: Reducing sympathetic stimulation of the heart, slowing SA/AV nodal activity
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Beta-blockade reduces sympathetic drive on cardiac pacemaker and conduction tissue.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Class III antiarrhythmic drugs primarily act by blocking:
o: Potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and the refractory period
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Class III drugs prolong the action potential/refractory period via potassium channel blockade.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Class IV antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem) primarily act by blocking:
o: L-type calcium channels, slowing AV nodal conduction
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Calcium channel blockers slow conduction through the calcium-dependent AV node.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The vector of normal ventricular depolarization is directed toward the:
o: Left, inferior, and posterior direction (roughly toward lead II)
Right side of the body exclusively
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The normal QRS axis points leftward/inferiorly, reflecting the dominant left ventricular mass.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Right axis deviation on ECG can be associated with:
o: Normal variant only in the elderly
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: An enlarged right ventricle shifts the electrical axis rightward.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Left axis deviation on ECG can be associated with:
o: Left ventricular hypertrophy or left anterior fascicular block
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: LVH or conduction abnormalities can shift the axis leftward.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: Sinus arrhythmia, a normal variant especially in young people, refers to:
o: An irregular heart rhythm unrelated to breathing
Variation in heart rate with the respiratory cycle (increasing with inspiration)
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is a benign, breathing-linked heart rate variation.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: The isoelectric TP segment on the ECG serves as the baseline reference for measuring:
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: The TP segment, being isoelectric, is the reference baseline for assessing ST deviation.

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.s: A widened QRS complex (>120 ms) is most suggestive of:
o: Bundle branch block or a ventricular origin of the beat
cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.e: Delayed ventricular activation, as in bundle branch block, widens the QRS.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Arteries, compared to veins, characteristically have:
o: Thicker muscular/elastic walls suited to handle high pressure
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Arteries withstand high pulsatile pressure via thicker, more elastic/muscular walls.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Veins, compared to arteries, characteristically have:
o: Valves to prevent backflow and thinner walls, acting as a blood volume reservoir
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Veins have valves and thin, compliant walls, holding most of the blood volume.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Capillaries are the site of exchange between blood and tissue primarily because they have:
o: A single layer of endothelium, allowing efficient diffusion
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: A thin single endothelial layer facilitates efficient diffusion exchange.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Arterioles are often called 'resistance vessels' because they:
o: Are the site of gas exchange
Have significant smooth muscle allowing them to constrict/dilate, major determinants of peripheral resistance
Have the largest total cross-sectional area
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Arteriolar smooth muscle tone is the principal regulator of systemic vascular resistance.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Total peripheral resistance is inversely related to vessel radius according to Poiseuille's law, such that resistance is proportional to:
o: 1 divided by radius to the fourth power
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius, making small changes highly impactful.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: The vasomotor center, controlling blood vessel tone, is located in the:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: The medullary vasomotor center integrates autonomic control of vascular tone.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Baroreceptor reflexes primarily provide:
o: No role in blood pressure control
Rapid, short-term, moment-to-moment blood pressure regulation
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Baroreceptors buffer rapid pressure fluctuations but adapt over longer periods.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Long-term blood pressure regulation depends predominantly on:
o: Renal control of blood volume via mechanisms such as the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Renal fluid/electrolyte handling is the dominant long-term blood pressure regulator.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Renin, released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney in response to decreased renal perfusion, catalyzes conversion of:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, the first RAAS step.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), mainly in the pulmonary vasculature, converts:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: ACE converts the relatively inactive angiotensin I into potent angiotensin II.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by causing:
o: Potent vasoconstriction and stimulation of aldosterone secretion
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that also stimulates aldosterone release.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Aldosterone, released from the adrenal cortex, raises blood pressure primarily by:
o: Promoting renal sodium (and water) reabsorption, increasing blood volume
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Aldosterone increases sodium (and secondary water) reabsorption, expanding blood volume.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin), released from the posterior pituitary, raises blood pressure via:
o: Renal water reabsorption (and at high levels, direct vasoconstriction)
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: ADH promotes water retention and, at high concentrations, vasoconstricts vessels.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), released from stretched atria, functions to:
o: Increase blood pressure and blood volume
Promote natriuresis and diuresis, lowering blood volume and pressure
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: ANP counters volume overload by promoting sodium/water excretion and vasodilation.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Local (intrinsic) regulation of blood flow that matches flow to a tissue's metabolic needs is termed:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Autoregulation locally matches blood flow to tissue metabolic demand.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Myogenic autoregulation of blood flow refers to the tendency of vascular smooth muscle to:
o: Relax when stretched by increased pressure
Dilate only in response to metabolites
Constrict in response to increased stretch/pressure, maintaining relatively constant flow
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Stretch-induced constriction (myogenic response) helps stabilize flow despite pressure changes.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Local metabolites that promote vasodilation in active tissue include:
o: Only nitric oxide with no other metabolites involved
Carbon dioxide, adenosine, potassium, and decreased pH (increased H+)
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Active tissue releases vasodilator metabolites that increase local blood flow.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Nitric oxide, released by vascular endothelium, causes:
o: Vasodilation via smooth muscle relaxation (through cGMP)
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Endothelial NO activates guanylate cyclase, raising cGMP and relaxing smooth muscle.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Endothelin, released by vascular endothelial cells, is one of the most potent known:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Endothelin is among the most powerful endogenous vasoconstrictors known.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Blood flow through an organ, according to a simplified form of Ohm's law applied to circulation, is proportional to:
o: Blood viscosity alone, independent of pressure
The pressure gradient across the vascular bed divided by resistance
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Flow = pressure gradient / resistance, analogous to Ohm's law.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Laminar blood flow, the normal smooth flow pattern, can become turbulent when:
o: Vessel diameter increases uniformly with no other changes
Velocity increases significantly, or vessel narrowing/roughness (e.g., atherosclerosis) disrupts flow
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: High velocity or irregular vessel walls disrupt smooth laminar flow, causing turbulence and murmurs.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: The majority of total blood volume at any given time is contained within the:
o: Veins (the venous system, acting as a capacitance reservoir)
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Veins hold roughly two-thirds of total blood volume at rest.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Postural (orthostatic) hypotension occurs when compensatory mechanisms fail to rapidly counteract:
o: Decreased heart rate upon standing only
Blood pooling in the lower limbs upon standing, which transiently decreases venous return and cardiac output
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Gravity-driven venous pooling on standing can transiently drop BP if reflexes are inadequate.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: The chemoreceptor reflex, involving peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies, primarily responds to:
o: Decreased oxygen, increased carbon dioxide, and decreased pH in the blood
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Peripheral chemoreceptors sense blood gas and pH changes, mainly hypoxia.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Severe hypoxia detected by peripheral chemoreceptors can trigger a reflex that, via the vasomotor center, tends to:
o: Only affect the respiratory system, never blood pressure
Increase sympathetic outflow, raising blood pressure and respiratory drive
Cause immediate bradycardia with hypotension in all cases
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Chemoreceptor-driven hypoxic response raises both respiratory and sympathetic vasomotor drive.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Capillary filtration and reabsorption are governed by Starling forces, which include:
o: Capillary hydrostatic pressure, interstitial hydrostatic pressure, plasma oncotic pressure, and interstitial oncotic pressure
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: All four Starling forces together determine net fluid movement across capillaries.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Lymphatic vessels help maintain fluid balance by:
o: Returning excess filtered interstitial fluid and protein back to the venous circulation
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Lymphatics recover fluid/protein that capillaries filter out, preventing edema.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Hypovolemic shock results primarily from:
o: Significant loss of blood volume, reducing venous return and cardiac output
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Volume loss directly reduces preload, venous return, and cardiac output.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Septic shock is characterized hemodynamically by:
o: Profound vasodilation (decreased systemic vascular resistance) often with initially increased cardiac output
Increased systemic vascular resistance and decreased cardiac output
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Sepsis classically causes distributive shock with low SVR and often high initial cardiac output.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Anaphylactic shock results from massive release of mediators like histamine, causing:
o: Widespread vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, leading to hypotension
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Histamine-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak cause profound distributive hypotension.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: The skin's blood flow is heavily influenced by the need for:
o: Thermoregulation, with sympathetic control of cutaneous vessels
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Cutaneous blood flow varies widely to help regulate body temperature.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Cerebral blood flow autoregulation maintains relatively constant flow across a range of arterial pressures primarily via:
o: No autoregulation exists in the brain
Myogenic and metabolic (e.g., CO2-sensitive) mechanisms intrinsic to cerebral vessels
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Intrinsic myogenic and metabolic mechanisms keep cerebral flow stable across a pressure range.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Increased arterial carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) causes cerebral vessels to:
o: Constrict only in the presence of hypoxia
Respond identically to skeletal muscle vessels
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Cerebral vessels are highly sensitive to CO2, dilating in response to hypercapnia.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Coronary blood flow autoregulation is heavily influenced by local:
o: Metabolic factors, especially adenosine released during myocardial hypoxia
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Adenosine release during increased myocardial metabolism is a key coronary vasodilator.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Exercise hyperemia (increased blood flow to active skeletal muscle) results primarily from:
o: Local metabolic vasodilation overriding sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Metabolite-driven local vasodilation predominates over sympathetic tone in active muscle.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Blood viscosity is significantly increased in conditions such as:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: An elevated hematocrit, as in polycythemia, raises blood viscosity.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: The velocity of blood flow is generally slowest in the:
o: Capillaries, due to their very large total cross-sectional area
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: The enormous combined cross-sectional area of capillaries slows flow velocity there, aiding exchange.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Varicose veins result primarily from:
o: Incompetent venous valves, leading to blood pooling and venous distension
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Failed venous valves allow backflow and pooling, dilating superficial veins.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: The primary determinant of coronary perfusion pressure to the left ventricle is the difference between aortic diastolic pressure and:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: Coronary perfusion pressure approximates aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure.

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.s: Blood pressure is defined as the product of cardiac output and:
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.e: BP = cardiac output x total peripheral resistance, a foundational hemodynamic relationship.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes) are characterized histologically by:
o: Multiple peripheral nuclei and no striations
A single central nucleus (occasionally two), striations, and intercalated discs
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Cardiomyocytes are striated, typically uninucleate, and joined by intercalated discs.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Intercalated discs contain which two types of specialized junctions important for cardiac function?
o: Desmosomes/fascia adherens (mechanical coupling) and gap junctions (electrical coupling)
Only gap junctions with no mechanical junctions
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Mechanical and electrical junctions together allow coordinated cardiac contraction.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The abundance of mitochondria in cardiomyocytes reflects their reliance on:
o: Creatine phosphate stores exclusively, with no oxidative metabolism
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Continuous contractile activity demands sustained oxidative ATP generation.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Purkinje fibers, part of the conduction system, are histologically distinguished from working myocardium by:
o: Being identical in every way to ventricular myocytes
Larger diameter, fewer myofibrils, and abundant glycogen, allowing rapid conduction
Presence of striations only in Purkinje fibers
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Purkinje fibers are specialized for rapid conduction rather than forceful contraction.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The endocardium, lining the inner surface of the heart chambers, is histologically similar to:
o: Vascular endothelium, being a simple squamous epithelium with underlying connective tissue
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Endocardium is continuous with, and histologically similar to, vascular endothelium.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The epicardium (visceral pericardium) is composed of:
o: A mesothelial layer overlying connective tissue, often containing coronary vessels and fat
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: The epicardium is a mesothelium-covered connective tissue layer, housing coronary vessels.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The heart develops from the primary heart tube, which forms by fusion of paired:
o: Endocardial tubes, derived from splanchnic mesoderm
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Paired endocardial tubes fuse in the midline to form the primitive heart tube.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Cardiac looping, an early step in heart development establishing left-right asymmetry, involves the heart tube bending to the:
o: Directly anterior with no lateral bending
It does not loop; it remains straight
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: The primitive heart tube normally loops to the right (D-looping).

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The interatrial septum develops through formation and subsequent modification of the septum primum and:
o: Septum secundum, together forming the foramen ovale mechanism
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Septum primum and septum secundum together create the valve-like foramen ovale.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The truncus arteriosus, an embryonic outflow structure, divides via spiral septation into the:
o: Left and right coronary arteries only
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: The aorticopulmonary (spiral) septum divides the truncus into aorta and pulmonary trunk.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Neural crest cells contribute importantly to the development of the:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Cardiac neural crest cells are essential for outflow tract septation.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The sinus venosus, an embryonic structure, is eventually incorporated mainly into the:
o: Right atrium (forming the smooth part, sinus venarum)
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: The sinus venosus becomes the smooth-walled portion of the right atrium.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Which embryonic vessel gives rise to the ductus arteriosus, connecting the pulmonary trunk to the aorta in fetal life?
o: Fourth aortic arch on the right side only
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: The left sixth aortic arch persists as the ductus arteriosus.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The fetal ductus arteriosus normally closes functionally shortly after birth due to:
o: Decreased blood flow through it before birth
Increased oxygen tension after breathing begins, causing smooth muscle constriction (with falling prostaglandin E levels)
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Rising postnatal oxygen and falling PGE2 trigger ductal smooth muscle constriction.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Indomethacin, a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor, can be used clinically to:
o: Promote closure of a patent ductus arteriosus
Keep a patent ductus arteriosus open
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Reducing PGE2 with indomethacin promotes ductal closure in a symptomatic PDA.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Prostaglandin E1 infusion is used clinically in certain congenital heart defects to:
o: Maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus, when systemic or pulmonary circulation is duct-dependent
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: PGE1 keeps the ductus open in duct-dependent congenital lesions, buying time before surgery.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Cholesterol, an important lipid in cardiovascular biochemistry, is synthesized primarily in the:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: The liver is the main site of endogenous cholesterol synthesis.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol is often termed 'bad cholesterol' because it:
o: Delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues and contributes to atherosclerotic plaque formation when elevated
Has no association with cardiovascular disease
Is not a lipoprotein at all
Removes cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Excess LDL deposits cholesterol in arterial walls, promoting atherosclerosis.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol is often termed 'good cholesterol' because it:
o: Participates in reverse cholesterol transport, removing cholesterol from tissues to the liver
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: HDL removes excess cholesterol from tissues, transporting it back to the liver.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial injury/dysfunction, followed by:
o: Lipid (LDL) accumulation in the intima, macrophage recruitment, and foam cell formation
Immediate rupture with no preceding process
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Endothelial injury permits lipid infiltration and an inflammatory cascade forming plaque.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Foam cells in atherosclerotic plaques are primarily:
o: Macrophages that have engulfed large amounts of oxidized LDL
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) are a hallmark of early atherosclerotic lesions.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Troponin I and T, released into the blood after myocardial infarction, are used clinically as:
o: Sensitive and specific biomarkers of myocardial injury
Markers of skeletal muscle injury only
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Cardiac troponins are the gold-standard biomarker for myocardial injury.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB), while less specific than troponin, is also used as a marker of:
o: Myocardial injury (though also found in some skeletal muscle)
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: CK-MB rises with myocardial damage, though with less tissue specificity than troponin.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), released from stretched ventricular myocardium, is clinically useful as a marker of:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: BNP rises with ventricular wall stress, aiding heart failure diagnosis.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Myocardial ischemia impairs ATP production, which can lead to:
o: Impaired ion pump function (e.g., Na+/K+-ATPase), cellular swelling, and eventually cell death if prolonged
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: ATP depletion disables ion pumps, disrupting homeostasis and eventually causing cell death.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Cardiac myocytes have very limited regenerative capacity after infarction, leading to replacement of dead tissue with:
o: New coronary vessels only, without scarring
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Infarcted myocardium heals by fibrosis rather than true myocyte regeneration.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Homocysteine, when elevated, is considered a risk factor for:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Hyperhomocysteinemia is associated with endothelial damage and elevated cardiovascular risk.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: C-reactive protein (CRP), an inflammatory marker, is associated with increased risk of:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Elevated CRP reflects systemic inflammation linked to atherosclerotic risk.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Statins lower LDL cholesterol primarily by inhibiting:
o: HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis and upregulating LDL receptors.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Nitrates, used to relieve angina, work by being converted to nitric oxide, which:
o: Dilates veins (reducing preload) and coronary arteries, improving oxygen supply-demand balance
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Nitrate-derived NO reduces preload and dilates coronary vessels, easing anginal symptoms.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: During myocardial infarction, anaerobic metabolism in ischemic tissue leads to accumulation of:
o: Lactate and hydrogen ions, lowering local pH
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Oxygen deprivation shifts metabolism to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate/acidosis.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The 'lub-dub' heart sounds, along with murmurs, can be graphically represented and correlated with pressure/volume changes in the:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: The Wiggers diagram correlates pressure, volume, ECG, and heart sounds across the cardiac cycle.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Cardiac hypertrophy in response to chronic pressure overload (e.g., hypertension) is typically:
o: Concentric hypertrophy, with increased wall thickness
Eccentric hypertrophy with chamber dilation primarily
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Pressure overload favors sarcomere addition in parallel, thickening the wall (concentric hypertrophy).

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Cardiac hypertrophy in response to chronic volume overload (e.g., valve regurgitation) is typically:
o: Eccentric hypertrophy, with chamber dilation and wall thickening
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Volume overload favors sarcomere addition in series, dilating the chamber (eccentric hypertrophy).

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Elevated triglycerides, along with high LDL and low HDL, form part of the lipid profile associated with:
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: This dyslipidemia pattern is a well-established cardiovascular risk profile.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The extracellular matrix of the heart, including fibroblasts and collagen, plays a role in:
o: Structural support and, when excessive (fibrosis), can impair cardiac function
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Matrix supports tissue architecture, but excess fibrosis stiffens and impairs the heart.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Myocardial fibrosis following infarction can predispose to:
o: Arrhythmias, due to disrupted electrical conduction through scar tissue
Complete return to normal electrical function
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Scar tissue disrupts normal conduction pathways, creating a substrate for arrhythmia.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) are counter-regulatory to which system, opposing its blood-pressure-raising effects?
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Natriuretic peptides oppose RAAS by promoting natriuresis, diuresis, and vasodilation.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: The coronary arteries are classified anatomically as end arteries because they:
o: Have limited functional collateral circulation, making occlusion likely to cause ischemia/infarction
Have extensive collateral circulation normally, preventing any ischemia
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Coronary arteries function largely as end arteries, so occlusion often causes significant infarction.

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.s: Reperfusion injury after restoring blood flow to ischemic myocardium can result from:
o: Immediate full functional recovery with no injury
Generation of reactive oxygen species and calcium overload upon reintroduction of oxygen
No additional cellular damage beyond the initial ischemia
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.e: Restoring oxygen can paradoxically generate ROS and calcium overload, worsening cell injury.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi at the level of:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The tracheal bifurcation (carina) lies at the sternal angle, roughly T4-T5.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The right main bronchus, compared to the left, is:
o: Identical in orientation to the left
More vertical, shorter, and wider, making it the more common site for aspirated foreign bodies
Longer and narrower than the left
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Its more vertical, wider, shorter course makes the right bronchus the classic aspiration site.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The right lung typically has how many lobes?
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The right lung has three lobes: upper, middle, and lower.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The left lung typically has how many lobes, accommodating the cardiac notch?
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The left lung has only two lobes (upper and lower), leaving room for the heart.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The pleura consists of two layers; the layer covering the lung surface directly is the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Visceral pleura is adherent directly to the lung surface.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The pleural cavity normally contains a small amount of fluid that functions to:
o: Reduce friction between the visceral and parietal pleura during breathing
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Pleural fluid lubricates the two pleural layers as they slide during respiration.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: A pneumothorax refers to:
o: Air accumulation in the pleural space, causing lung collapse
Pus in the pleural space specifically
Fluid accumulation in the pleural space
Blood accumulation in the pleural space specifically
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Air entering the pleural space disrupts the negative pressure, collapsing the lung.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The diaphragm is innervated by the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The phrenic nerve, from cervical roots C3-C5, is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The diaphragm has three major openings; the opening at approximately T8 transmits the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The caval opening at T8 transmits the inferior vena cava.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm is located at approximately which vertebral level?
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The esophageal hiatus, transmitting the esophagus and vagal trunks, sits at T10.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, transmitting the aorta and thoracic duct, is located at approximately:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The aortic hiatus, the most posterior/inferior opening, is at T12.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The larynx's primary cartilage, providing the laryngeal prominence ('Adam's apple'), is the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The thyroid cartilage forms the anterior laryngeal prominence.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway, forming a signet-ring shape, is the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The cricoid cartilage is the sole complete ring, unlike the C-shaped tracheal cartilages.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The epiglottis functions primarily to:
o: Cover the laryngeal inlet during swallowing, preventing aspiration
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The epiglottis folds over the larynx during swallowing to protect the airway.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The vocal cords (folds) are primarily controlled by muscles innervated by the:
o: Superior laryngeal nerve exclusively for all muscles
Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus) for most intrinsic muscles
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles controlling the vocal folds.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve classically results in:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Recurrent laryngeal nerve damage impairs vocal cord movement, causing hoarseness.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The conducting zone of the respiratory tract includes structures from the trachea to the:
o: Terminal bronchioles, with no gas exchange occurring
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The conducting zone ends at terminal bronchioles, purely transporting air.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The respiratory zone, where gas exchange occurs, begins at the:
o: Terminal bronchioles exclusively without further branching
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Respiratory bronchioles mark the start of the gas-exchanging respiratory zone.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Alveolar type I cells primarily function for:
o: Gas exchange, forming the thin structure for diffusion
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Thin type I pneumocytes cover most of the alveolar surface, optimized for diffusion.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Alveolar type II cells primarily function to:
o: Provide the thin gas exchange surface
Phagocytose debris as the main function
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Type II pneumocytes synthesize and secrete surfactant, and can regenerate type I cells.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Pulmonary surfactant's primary function is to:
o: Facilitate gas exchange directly by diffusion enhancement
Reduce alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis)
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Surfactant lowers surface tension, stabilizing alveoli against collapse.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) function to:
o: Phagocytose inhaled particles and pathogens within the alveoli
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Alveolar macrophages are the resident immune cells clearing debris from alveolar spaces.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The blood supply to the lung parenchyma for gas exchange comes from the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to alveolar capillaries for gas exchange.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The bronchial arteries, branches of the aorta, supply:
o: The bronchial tree and connective tissue (nutritive blood supply)
The pulmonary capillaries directly for gas exchange
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Bronchial arteries provide the nutritive (not gas-exchanging) blood supply to airway walls.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The phrenic nerve arises from which cervical spinal nerve roots?
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive' - the phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The costodiaphragmatic recess is a potential space where:
o: The parietal pleura reflects between costal and diaphragmatic surfaces, and fluid tends to accumulate
The lungs always fully occupy during quiet breathing
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: This recess is a common site for pleural fluid to pool, especially when supine or upright.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The hilum of the lung is where structures including the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, and pulmonary veins:
