respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The hilum is the entry/exit point for the root structures of each lung.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The right lung's horizontal fissure separates the:
o: There is no horizontal fissure in the right lung
All three lobes simultaneously in one plane
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The horizontal fissure divides the right upper and middle lobes.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The oblique fissure, present in both lungs, separates the:
o: Upper and middle lobes only (right lung)
Only the two lungs from each other
The lower lobe from the upper (and middle, in the right lung) lobe(s)
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The oblique fissure separates the lower lobe from the lobe(s) above it in both lungs.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The nasal cavity and upper airway function to:
o: Warm, humidify, and filter inspired air before it reaches the lower airway
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The upper airway conditions inspired air before it reaches the delicate lower respiratory tract.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The paranasal sinuses include the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The four paranasal sinus groups are frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Cartilage support in the trachea and bronchi decreases progressively toward the periphery, being absent in the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Bronchioles lack cartilage, relying instead on smooth muscle and elastic tissue.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Goblet cells in the respiratory epithelium function to:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles for mucociliary clearance.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The mucociliary escalator, moving trapped particles out of the airway, relies on:
o: Coordinated ciliary beating of respiratory epithelium moving mucus upward toward the pharynx
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Cilia beat in coordinated waves, propelling the mucus blanket toward the throat for clearance.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The respiratory epithelium lining most of the conducting airways is classified as:
o: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: This epithelium type lines the trachea and bronchi, supporting mucociliary clearance.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The mediastinal structures at risk during a needle thoracostomy for tension pneumothorax (2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line) include avoiding injury to the:
o: Intercostal neurovascular bundle, which runs along the inferior border of each rib
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Needles are inserted just above a rib's superior border to avoid the neurovascular bundle below each rib.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The apex of each lung extends above the level of the:
o: First rib/clavicle into the root of the neck
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The lung apex projects into the neck, above the first rib and clavicle.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: The base of the lung rests upon the:
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: The concave base of each lung sits on the corresponding dome of the diaphragm.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Accessory muscles of inspiration, used during labored breathing, include the:
o: Latissimus dorsi as the primary accessory muscle
Diaphragm exclusively, with no accessory muscles used
Internal intercostals and abdominal muscles primarily
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Sternocleidomastoid and scalenes elevate the rib cage during forced/labored inspiration.

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.s: Expiration during quiet breathing is normally:
o: An active process requiring significant muscle contraction
Dependent entirely on abdominal muscle contraction
Driven by the intercostal muscles only
A passive process, relying on elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.e: Quiet expiration relies on passive elastic recoil once inspiratory muscles relax.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Tidal volume is defined as:
o: The volume of air moved in or out of the lungs during a normal, quiet breath
The volume exhaled forcefully after maximal inspiration
The maximum volume that can be inhaled after a normal inspiration
The volume remaining in the lungs after maximal expiration
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Tidal volume is the air moved per normal resting breath, about 500 mL in adults.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Residual volume is defined as:
o: Total lung capacity minus vital capacity is unrelated to residual volume
The volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal forced expiration
The volume inhaled during maximal inspiration
The maximal volume that can be exhaled after normal inspiration
The air moved during a normal breath
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Residual volume is the air that can never be exhaled, keeping alveoli open.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Vital capacity is defined as:
o: Residual volume plus tidal volume only
The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration (IRV + TV + ERV)
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Vital capacity sums inspiratory reserve, tidal, and expiratory reserve volumes.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Total lung capacity equals:
o: Tidal volume plus residual volume only
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: TLC = VC + RV, the sum of all lung volumes.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is defined as:
o: Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume
The volume remaining in the lungs after a normal, quiet expiration (ERV + RV)
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: FRC is the resting lung volume after passive expiration, combining ERV and RV.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Anatomical dead space refers to:
o: Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused
The volume of the conducting airways where no gas exchange occurs
Alveoli that are perfused but not ventilated
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Anatomical dead space is the conducting airway volume that never reaches gas-exchanging surfaces.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Physiological dead space includes anatomical dead space plus:
o: Alveolar dead space (ventilated but poorly/non-perfused alveoli)
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Physiological dead space adds any alveoli that are ventilated without adequate perfusion.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Boyle's law, relevant to pulmonary ventilation, states that at constant temperature:
o: Pressure and volume are directly proportional
Volume and temperature are inversely proportional
Pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional
Gas volume is constant regardless of pressure
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Boyle's law underlies how thoracic volume changes drive pressure changes that move air.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: During inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction increases thoracic volume, which (by Boyle's law) causes intrapulmonary pressure to:
o: Equal intrapleural pressure exactly at all times
Decrease below atmospheric pressure, drawing air into the lungs
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Expanding thoracic volume drops alveolar pressure below atmospheric, driving inspiratory airflow.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Intrapleural pressure is normally:
o: Equal to alveolar pressure at all times
Higher than alveolar pressure during inspiration
Negative relative to atmospheric pressure, helping keep the lungs expanded against their elastic recoil
Positive relative to atmospheric pressure throughout the respiratory cycle
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Negative intrapleural pressure counters the lung's inward elastic recoil, keeping it inflated.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Lung compliance refers to:
o: The force required to move air through the airways
The ease with which the lungs expand for a given change in pressure (change in volume/change in pressure)
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Compliance measures how readily the lung expands per unit pressure change.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Decreased lung compliance, as seen in pulmonary fibrosis, means the lungs:
o: Are stiffer, requiring greater pressure changes to achieve a given volume change
Are unaffected in their mechanical properties
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Fibrotic lungs are stiff, needing more pressure to inflate to a given volume.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Increased lung compliance, as seen in emphysema, is associated with:
o: Loss of elastic recoil, making lungs easier to inflate but harder to passively deflate
Stiffer lungs requiring more pressure to inflate
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Destroyed elastic tissue in emphysema increases compliance but impairs passive recoil-driven expiration.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Surfactant reduces surface tension in alveoli, which:
o: Has no effect on lung mechanics
Decreases the work of breathing and helps prevent alveolar collapse, especially in smaller alveoli
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Lower surface tension eases lung inflation and stabilizes small alveoli against collapse.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: According to LaPlace's law applied to alveoli, for a given surface tension, smaller alveoli would have a tendency to:
o: Have lower collapsing pressure than larger alveoli
Have no relationship between size and pressure
Have higher collapsing pressure than larger alveoli, risking collapse into larger ones without surfactant
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Without surfactant, LaPlace's law predicts smaller alveoli would collapse into larger ones.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome results primarily from:
o: Insufficient surfactant production due to lung immaturity, especially in premature infants
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Immature type II pneumocytes in preemies produce too little surfactant, causing alveolar collapse.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Airway resistance is primarily determined by the:
o: Radius of the airway (inversely, to the fourth power, similar to vascular resistance)
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Small changes in airway radius produce large changes in resistance, per Poiseuille's law.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Bronchoconstriction, as in an asthma attack, primarily affects pulmonary mechanics by:
o: Increasing airway resistance, making expiration particularly difficult
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Narrowed airways sharply raise resistance, especially limiting expiratory airflow.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) divided by forced vital capacity (FVC) is used to distinguish:
o: Upper from lower respiratory tract infection
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: The FEV1/FVC ratio is the key spirometric tool separating obstructive from restrictive patterns.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (below approximately 0.7) is characteristic of:
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Airflow obstruction disproportionately reduces FEV1, lowering the FEV1/FVC ratio.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Restrictive lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis) typically show:
o: Reduced lung volumes (including FVC and TLC) with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1/FVC ratio with normal or increased lung volumes
Increased residual volume primarily with normal FVC
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Restrictive disease shrinks lung volumes proportionally, keeping the FEV1/FVC ratio normal or high.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: The work of breathing is primarily used to overcome:
o: Elastic resistance of lung tissue and airway (frictional) resistance to airflow
Muscle fatigue exclusively, unrelated to mechanics
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Breathing work is spent against elastic recoil and airway resistance to airflow.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Intra-alveolar pressure at the end of inspiration and end of expiration (points of no airflow) equals:
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: With no airflow, alveolar pressure equilibrates with atmospheric pressure.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: During forced expiration, intrapleural pressure can become:
o: Positive, potentially exceeding airway pressure and causing dynamic airway compression
Always more negative than at rest
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Forced expiration raises intrapleural pressure, which can compress airways dynamically.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Dynamic airway compression during forced expiration particularly affects patients with:
o: Obstructive lung disease (e.g., emphysema), due to loss of airway support/elastic recoil
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Loss of elastic tethering in emphysema makes airways especially prone to dynamic collapse.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Pursed-lip breathing, often used by COPD patients, helps by:
o: Creating back-pressure that helps prevent dynamic airway collapse during expiration
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Exhaling against pursed lips raises downstream pressure, splinting airways open longer.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: The transpulmonary pressure is defined as the difference between:
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Transpulmonary pressure is the distending pressure keeping the lung inflated.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: A pneumothorax causes lung collapse because:
o: Air enters the pleural space, eliminating the normally negative intrapleural pressure that keeps the lung expanded
Blood flow to the lung stops
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Loss of the negative pleural pressure allows the lung's own elastic recoil to collapse it.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Minute ventilation is calculated as:
o: Residual volume multiplied by respiratory rate
Vital capacity multiplied by respiratory rate
Tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate
Tidal volume divided by respiratory rate
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Minute ventilation = tidal volume x breaths per minute.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Alveolar ventilation, more physiologically relevant than minute ventilation, is calculated as:
o: Minute ventilation divided by dead space
Vital capacity divided by respiratory rate
(Tidal volume minus dead space volume) multiplied by respiratory rate
Residual volume multiplied by respiratory rate
Tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Alveolar ventilation subtracts dead space air, reflecting gas actually reaching alveoli.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Rapid, shallow breathing (compared to slow, deep breathing at the same minute ventilation) results in:
o: Decreased alveolar ventilation, since a greater fraction of each breath ventilates dead space
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Fixed dead space takes a bigger bite out of small tidal volumes, lowering alveolar ventilation.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: The chest wall's natural tendency, if not opposed by the lungs, would be to:
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: The chest wall's inherent elastic tendency is to spring outward.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: The lung's natural tendency, if not opposed by the chest wall, would be to:
o: Collapse inward due to its own elastic recoil
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: The lung's elastic tissue and surface tension favor collapse if unopposed.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: At functional residual capacity, the opposing elastic forces of the lung (inward recoil) and chest wall (outward recoil) are:
o: Maximally different, causing rapid volume change
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: FRC is the resting volume where these two opposing elastic forces balance.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is a simple measure often used to monitor:
o: Airway obstruction severity, particularly in asthma
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: PEFR is a simple bedside/home tool for tracking asthma control and severity.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Spirometry can directly measure all lung volumes and capacities except those that include:
o: Residual volume (and any capacity containing it, e.g., FRC, TLC), which require other methods like helium dilution
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Spirometry cannot measure the air that remains after maximal exhalation, requiring dilution/plethysmography techniques.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: The Bohr equation is used to calculate:
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: The Bohr equation estimates physiological dead space from expired and arterial CO2.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Increased airway resistance from mucus plugging or bronchoconstriction primarily increases the:
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Narrowed airways raise the frictional component of the work of breathing.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: A flail chest, from multiple rib fractures, causes paradoxical chest wall movement, which:
o: Has no effect on breathing mechanics
Impairs effective ventilation, as the flail segment moves inward during inspiration
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: The unstable segment moves opposite to the rest of the chest wall, impairing effective ventilation.

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.s: Obesity can impair pulmonary mechanics primarily by:
o: Reducing chest wall compliance and functional residual capacity due to increased mass loading
Having no mechanical effect on breathing
respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.e: Excess chest/abdominal mass restricts chest wall movement, lowering FRC and compliance.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane occurs primarily by:
o: Simple diffusion, driven by partial pressure gradients
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: O2 and CO2 move passively down their partial pressure gradients by simple diffusion.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is normally approximately:
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Alveolar PO2 is normally around 100 mmHg.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in alveolar air/arterial blood is normally approximately:
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Normal arterial/alveolar PCO2 is approximately 40 mmHg.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Diffusion of gases across the respiratory membrane is enhanced by which membrane characteristics (Fick's law)?
o: Large thickness and small surface area
Large surface area and small (thin) diffusion distance
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Fick's law favors diffusion with large area, thin membrane, and steep partial pressure gradient.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Carbon dioxide diffuses across the respiratory membrane more readily than oxygen mainly because CO2:
o: Does not need to cross a membrane
Has a much higher partial pressure gradient
Has much higher solubility in the membrane/plasma, despite similar molecular weight
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: CO2's greater solubility more than compensates for its slightly larger molecular size, aiding diffusion.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Approximately what percentage of oxygen in blood is transported bound to hemoglobin (versus dissolved in plasma)?
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: The vast majority (~98-99%) of blood oxygen is hemoglobin-bound, not dissolved.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Each hemoglobin molecule can bind a maximum of how many oxygen molecules?
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Hemoglobin's four heme groups each bind one oxygen molecule.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve's sigmoidal shape reflects:
o: No relationship between PO2 and saturation
Only relevant to myoglobin, not hemoglobin
Cooperative binding, where binding of one oxygen molecule increases hemoglobin's affinity for subsequent oxygen molecules
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Cooperativity among hemoglobin's subunits produces the characteristic sigmoid curve.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: A rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve indicates:
o: Decreased hemoglobin affinity for oxygen, favoring O2 unloading to tissues
Increased oxygen binding at the lungs specifically
A pathological state only, never physiological
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: A rightward shift lowers affinity, promoting oxygen release where tissues need it most.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Factors causing a rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve include:
o: Increased temperature, increased 2,3-BPG, and acidosis (increased CO2/H+)
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Active, acidic, warm tissue conditions shift the curve right, aiding oxygen delivery.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) has a left-shifted oxygen dissociation curve compared to adult hemoglobin, meaning it has:
o: Higher oxygen affinity than HbA, facilitating oxygen transfer from maternal to fetal blood
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: HbF's higher affinity helps it extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood in three main forms: dissolved in plasma, as carbaminohemoglobin, and predominantly as:
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: The majority of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate after conversion in red blood cells.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The enzyme carbonic anhydrase, found in red blood cells, catalyzes the reaction:
o: CO2 + H2O to carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates to H+ and HCO3-
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Carbonic anhydrase rapidly interconverts CO2/water and carbonic acid, enabling bicarbonate transport.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The chloride shift refers to the exchange of chloride ions for:
o: Sodium ions across the red cell membrane
Bicarbonate ions across the red cell membrane, maintaining electrical neutrality
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: As bicarbonate exits red cells, chloride enters to preserve electroneutrality (the Hamburger shift).

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The Haldane effect describes how:
o: Describes oxygen transport exclusively, not CO2
Oxygenation of hemoglobin increases its affinity for CO2/H+ (favoring CO2 unloading in the lungs)
Deoxygenated hemoglobin has increased affinity for CO2 and H+, facilitating CO2 loading in tissues; oxygenation in the lungs then facilitates CO2 release
CO2 has no effect on hemoglobin's oxygen affinity
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: The Haldane effect links hemoglobin's oxygenation state to its CO2-carrying capacity.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Carbon monoxide poisoning is dangerous because carbon monoxide:
o: Is not absorbed into the bloodstream
Binds hemoglobin with much greater affinity than oxygen, displacing oxygen and impairing its release to tissues
Has lower affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: CO's very high hemoglobin affinity both blocks O2 binding and impairs O2 release from remaining sites.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient is used clinically to help distinguish:
o: Causes of hypoxemia, such as V/Q mismatch/shunt versus hypoventilation
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: A widened A-a gradient points to a lung-based cause of hypoxemia rather than pure hypoventilation.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) matching is optimal for gas exchange; a V/Q ratio of zero indicates:
o: No blood flow and no ventilation
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: A V/Q of zero means blood flows past alveoli that receive no ventilation - a shunt.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: A V/Q ratio approaching infinity indicates:
o: Complete airway obstruction with normal perfusion
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: An infinite V/Q ratio describes ventilated alveoli receiving no blood flow - dead space.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: In the upright lung, ventilation and perfusion are both greater at the base than the apex, but the V/Q ratio is:
o: Higher at the apex than the base, since perfusion decreases more than ventilation toward the apex
Higher at the base than the apex
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Perfusion falls off faster than ventilation up the lung, raising the V/Q ratio toward the apex.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is a unique pulmonary vascular response that:
o: Diverts blood flow away from poorly ventilated (hypoxic) alveoli toward better-ventilated areas, optimizing V/Q matching
Increases blood flow to poorly ventilated alveoli
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Unlike systemic vessels, pulmonary vessels constrict in hypoxia to redirect flow toward better-ventilated regions.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, as in COPD, can lead to:
o: Pulmonary hypertension and eventual right heart strain (cor pulmonale)
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Widespread chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction raises pulmonary pressures, straining the right heart.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Diffusion-limited gas exchange, as opposed to perfusion-limited, is exemplified in health mainly by:
o: Carbon monoxide (used to measure diffusion capacity, DLCO)
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: CO's high hemoglobin affinity keeps its plasma partial pressure low, making it diffusion-limited, useful for DLCO testing.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Under normal resting conditions, oxygen uptake across the alveolar-capillary membrane is typically:
o: Perfusion-limited, with equilibration occurring well before the end of the pulmonary capillary
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: At rest, oxygen equilibrates quickly, so flow (perfusion) becomes the limiting factor, not diffusion.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: During strenuous exercise or in diseases thickening the alveolar membrane, oxygen exchange can become:
o: Diffusion-limited, as equilibration may not be complete by the end of the capillary transit time
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Faster transit time or a thickened membrane can prevent full equilibration, making exchange diffusion-limited.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Oxygen content of blood depends on hemoglobin concentration, oxygen saturation, and:
o: A small contribution from dissolved oxygen (based on PO2 and solubility)
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Total oxygen content combines hemoglobin-bound oxygen with a small dissolved fraction.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity of blood primarily by:
o: Having no effect on oxygen transport
Increasing 2,3-BPG only, with no effect on capacity
Decreasing the total amount of hemoglobin available to bind oxygen, even if saturation is normal
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Less hemoglobin means less total oxygen carried, even at normal percent saturation.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Methemoglobin, an abnormal form of hemoglobin, impairs oxygen transport because its iron is:
o: Oxidized to the ferric (Fe3+) state, which cannot bind oxygen effectively
In the normal ferrous (Fe2+) state, functioning normally
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Methemoglobin's oxidized iron cannot bind oxygen, reducing effective oxygen transport.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The respiratory quotient (RQ), the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed, is approximately what value for a mixed diet?
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: A typical mixed diet yields an RQ of about 0.8.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: A respiratory quotient of 1.0 suggests predominant metabolism of:
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Pure carbohydrate oxidation produces an RQ of 1.0.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is typically reduced in conditions that:
o: Increase pulmonary capillary blood volume only
Thicken or destroy the alveolar-capillary membrane (e.g., fibrosis, emphysema)
Have no effect on the diffusion barrier
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Membrane thickening or destruction of exchange surface lowers DLCO.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Oxygen saturation (SaO2) as measured by pulse oximetry reflects:
o: Total oxygen content directly, unaffected by hemoglobin level
The percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen
The partial pressure of oxygen dissolved in plasma directly
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Pulse oximetry estimates the fraction of hemoglobin sites that are oxygen-bound.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: A patient can have normal oxygen saturation but significantly reduced oxygen content if they have:
o: Severe anemia (reduced hemoglobin, even if the available hemoglobin is well saturated)
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Saturation reflects percent of available hemoglobin bound, not the total hemoglobin/oxygen amount.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The partial pressure of oxygen in mixed venous blood returning to the lungs is normally approximately:
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Mixed venous PO2 is typically around 40 mmHg after tissue oxygen extraction.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: High altitude exposure causes hypoxemia primarily due to:
o: Decreased barometric (and thus inspired oxygen partial) pressure
Increased carbon dioxide levels in the air
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Lower barometric pressure at altitude reduces the partial pressure of inspired oxygen, though its percentage is unchanged.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Chronic exposure to high altitude induces compensatory:
o: Increased erythropoietin, increased red cell mass, and increased 2,3-BPG
Decreased renal excretion of bicarbonate exclusively
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Chronic hypoxia drives erythropoietin-mediated polycythemia and increased 2,3-BPG to aid oxygen delivery.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Cyanosis, a bluish discoloration of skin/mucosa, typically becomes clinically apparent when deoxygenated hemoglobin exceeds approximately:
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Cyanosis classically appears once deoxyhemoglobin exceeds roughly 5 g/dL.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Central cyanosis (affecting mucous membranes) typically indicates:
o: Purely peripheral vasoconstriction with normal oxygenation
Excess carbon dioxide only, without hypoxemia
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Central cyanosis reflects true systemic arterial desaturation, unlike peripheral cyanosis from local vasoconstriction.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: Oxygen therapy is used cautiously in some chronic CO2 retainers (e.g., severe COPD) because:
o: It has no effect on ventilation
It can blunt hypoxic respiratory drive in patients dependent on it, though this concern should not withhold needed oxygen in acute hypoxemia
It converts oxygen to carbon monoxide
Oxygen has no clinical benefit for hypoxemia
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: Some chronic CO2 retainers rely more on hypoxic drive, so excess oxygen requires careful titration.

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.s: The Bohr effect and Haldane effect together illustrate how gas transport for oxygen and carbon dioxide are:
o: Interrelated, each gas's binding influencing the other's affinity for hemoglobin
Completely independent processes with no interaction
respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.e: These complementary effects couple oxygen and CO2 transport at the tissues and lungs respectively.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The primary respiratory rhythm-generating center is located in the:
o: Medulla oblongata (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups)
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Medullary respiratory groups generate the basic automatic breathing rhythm.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The pontine respiratory centers (pneumotaxic and apneustic centers) primarily function to:
o: Generate the basic respiratory rhythm independently
Modulate/fine-tune the rhythm generated by the medulla, influencing the transition between inspiration and expiration
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Pontine centers refine the medullary rhythm rather than generating it themselves.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The pneumotaxic center in the pons functions to:
o: Have no effect on breathing pattern
Limit inspiration, helping to switch off inspiration and increase respiratory rate
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: The pneumotaxic center inhibits inspiration, shaping breath timing and rate.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Central chemoreceptors, located near the ventral surface of the medulla, primarily respond to:
o: Changes in cerebrospinal fluid H+ concentration, reflecting arterial CO2 levels
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: CO2 crosses into CSF and lowers pH there, which central chemoreceptors detect.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Central chemoreceptors are the primary drivers of ventilation under normal conditions, responding most sensitively to changes in:
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: CO2, via central chemoreceptors, is the dominant regulator of minute-to-minute ventilation.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) are the primary sensors of:
o: Blood pressure primarily, not respiratory gases
Arterial oxygen (particularly significant hypoxemia), as well as CO2 and pH
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Peripheral chemoreceptors are uniquely sensitive to falling arterial oxygen.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The carotid bodies are located at the:
o: Bifurcation of the common carotid artery
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Carotid bodies sit at the common carotid bifurcation, sensing arterial blood directly.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: In chronic CO2 retainers, the primary ventilatory drive can shift to depend more heavily on:
o: Central chemoreceptor CO2 sensitivity, which remains fully intact
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Chronic CO2 elevation can blunt central chemoreceptor sensitivity, shifting reliance toward hypoxic drive.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The Hering-Breuer inflation reflex, mediated by stretch receptors in the lung, functions to:
o: Inhibit further inspiration when the lungs are sufficiently inflated, preventing overinflation
Stimulate the pneumotaxic center to prolong inspiration
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Pulmonary stretch receptors signal to stop inspiration once the lung is adequately filled.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Irritant receptors in the airway epithelium, when stimulated by noxious substances, trigger:
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Irritant receptors defend the airway via reflex bronchoconstriction and coughing.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: J-receptors (juxtacapillary receptors), located near pulmonary capillaries, are stimulated by:
o: Pulmonary capillary congestion/edema, causing rapid shallow breathing
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: J-receptors respond to interstitial/capillary congestion, producing characteristic rapid shallow breathing.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Voluntary control of breathing (e.g., breath-holding, speech) originates from the:
o: Cerebral cortex, which can override (within limits) the automatic brainstem rhythm
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Cortical pathways allow conscious, temporary override of the automatic breathing rhythm.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Breath-holding time is ultimately limited primarily by rising:
o: Arterial CO2 (and falling O2), which eventually overrides voluntary control
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Rising CO2 (and falling O2) eventually forces resumption of breathing despite voluntary effort.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Hyperventilation causing a decrease in arterial CO2 (hypocapnia) can lead to:
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Low CO2 constricts cerebral vessels, reducing cerebral blood flow and causing lightheadedness.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Cheyne-Stokes respiration, a pattern of alternating hyperventilation and apnea, is often associated with:
o: Heart failure or central nervous system disorders affecting respiratory control
Normal healthy breathing during sleep in all people
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Delayed feedback to respiratory centers, as in heart failure, produces this crescendo-decrescendo pattern.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Apneustic breathing, characterized by prolonged inspiratory gasps, can result from damage to the:
o: Lower pons (apneustic center), especially with loss of vagal and pneumotaxic input
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Loss of inhibitory pontine/vagal input can unmask prolonged apneustic inspiratory gasps.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Exercise-induced hyperventilation is regulated by multiple factors including:
o: Neural feedforward signals from the motor cortex and feedback from muscle/joint receptors, in addition to chemoreceptor input
No specific regulation; ventilation is unrelated to exercise
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Exercise ventilation integrates anticipatory cortical signals with peripheral feedback, not just chemoreceptors.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: During moderate exercise, arterial blood gases (PaO2, PaCO2) typically remain:
o: Remarkably stable/near normal, despite large increases in ventilation and metabolic demand
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Ventilation increases proportionally with metabolic demand, keeping blood gases near normal during moderate exercise.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Sleep apnea, characterized by repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, can be classified as obstructive or:
o: Central (due to impaired respiratory drive from the brain)
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Sleep apnea is broadly divided into obstructive and central types.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Obstructive sleep apnea results from:
o: Failure of the brain to signal breathing
Physical collapse/obstruction of the upper airway during sleep, despite intact respiratory drive
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: OSA involves mechanical airway collapse, not a failure of central respiratory drive.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Central sleep apnea results from:
o: Impaired central nervous system respiratory drive, with reduced or absent effort to breathe
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: CSA reflects a failure of the brain to generate adequate respiratory effort.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Newborn infants have a respiratory rate that is:
o: Faster than adults, gradually decreasing with age
Absent for the first hours of life normally
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Neonates breathe considerably faster than adults, slowing progressively through childhood.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The initial breath of a newborn is triggered by multiple stimuli including:
o: No specific trigger; it is entirely reflexive with no chemical stimulus
Hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, cold stimulation, and tactile stimuli after birth
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Multiple chemical and physical stimuli converge to trigger the newborn's first breath.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Respiratory centers integrate input to maintain relatively stable arterial CO2, making CO2 the primary regulated variable in:
o: Never; oxygen is always the primary regulated variable
Normal, healthy individuals under most conditions
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: In health, ventilation is tuned mainly to keep arterial CO2 stable, not oxygen.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Metabolic acidosis stimulates ventilation (Kussmaul breathing) primarily via:
o: Only central chemoreceptors, since CO2 does not change
Both central and peripheral chemoreceptors sensing decreased pH, with peripheral chemoreceptors responding more rapidly to blood pH changes
Central chemoreceptors responding to CSF pH changes and peripheral chemoreceptors responding to blood pH
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Both chemoreceptor types sense the falling pH, with peripheral receptors reacting faster to blood pH itself.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Kussmaul breathing, deep and labored breathing seen in diabetic ketoacidosis, functions to:
o: Blow off CO2, partially compensating for the metabolic acidosis
Have no relationship to acid-base status
Increase blood pH abnormally with no compensatory role
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Deep respirations lower CO2, providing respiratory compensation for the underlying metabolic acidosis.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Opioid overdose is dangerous partly because opioids:
o: Depress the medullary respiratory centers, reducing respiratory rate and drive, risking respiratory failure
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Opioids blunt medullary CO2 sensitivity and respiratory drive, risking fatal hypoventilation.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The Hering-Breuer deflation reflex, less prominent than the inflation reflex, is thought to:
o: Stimulate inspiratory effort when the lungs are deflated
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: This reflex is thought to promote inspiratory effort when lung volume is low.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Chemoreceptor sensitivity to CO2 can be blunted by:
o: Acute exposure to high CO2 only
Normal healthy aging with no other cause
Chronic CO2 retention (as in COPD), leading to renal compensation and relative desensitization
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Chronic hypercapnia with renal bicarbonate compensation can blunt central chemoreceptor CO2 sensitivity.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The respiratory centers receive input from higher brain centers during emotional states (e.g., fear, pain), which can cause:
o: Altered breathing patterns such as gasping or breath-holding, independent of metabolic need
Only changes in heart rate, never breathing
Complete cessation of the medullary rhythm permanently
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Limbic/cortical input can alter breathing patterns independent of chemical drive.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Carotid body chemoreceptor activity increases significantly when arterial PO2 falls below approximately:
o: 60 mmHg, with a steep response below this threshold
There is no threshold; response is linear from 100 mmHg downward
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Carotid body output rises sharply once PO2 drops below roughly 60 mmHg.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Doming of the diaphragm and its excursion during quiet breathing are typically around:
o: No movement occurs during quiet breathing
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: During quiet tidal breathing, the diaphragm moves only about 1-2 cm.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Panting, seen in some animals for thermoregulation, involves rapid shallow breathing that primarily ventilates:
o: Only the alveoli with no dead space involvement
Mainly the dead space (upper airway), allowing heat loss without significant changes in alveolar ventilation/blood gases
The alveoli extensively, causing significant changes in blood gases
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Panting mostly moves air through dead space, dissipating heat without disturbing alveolar gas exchange.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The apneustic center's normal inhibitory input, when removed (as in certain brainstem lesions), can result in:
o: Apneustic breathing, with prolonged inspiratory gasps
Increased respiratory rate with normal pattern
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Without pontine/vagal inhibition, unopposed apneustic activity produces prolonged inspiratory gasps.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Ondine's curse (congenital central hypoventilation syndrome) is characterized by:
o: Loss of automatic control of breathing, particularly during sleep, while voluntary control remains relatively intact
Normal voluntary and automatic breathing control
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: This rare disorder selectively impairs automatic breathing control, especially during sleep.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: The medullary respiratory neurons project to which structures to effect breathing?
o: Spinal motor neurons innervating the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Medullary output descends to spinal motor neurons controlling respiratory muscles.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Increased body temperature (fever) tends to:
o: Increase respiratory rate, partly as a heat-dissipating mechanism and increased metabolic rate
Only affect heart rate, not breathing
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: Fever raises metabolic rate and respiratory rate, partly aiding heat loss.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: During REM sleep, breathing typically becomes:
o: More irregular, with possible brief pauses, partly due to reduced input from voluntary/behavioral influences and postural muscle atonia
Identical to wakefulness in every respect
Slower and deeper than wakefulness consistently
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: REM sleep is associated with irregular breathing patterns and generalized muscle atonia.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor sometimes used for altitude sickness, works partly by:
o: Promoting bicarbonate excretion by the kidney, causing a mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation, aiding acclimatization
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: By inducing mild metabolic acidosis, acetazolamide drives compensatory hyperventilation, aiding altitude acclimatization.

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.s: Overall, respiratory control integrates chemical (blood gas/pH) and neural (behavioral, reflex) inputs at the level of the:
o: Brainstem respiratory centers, which coordinate output to respiratory muscles
Peripheral nerves exclusively without central integration
respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.e: The brainstem integrates all chemical and neural inputs to generate coordinated respiratory output.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: The respiratory epithelium of the trachea and bronchi is classified as:
o: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: This ciliated, mucus-secreting epithelium lines the conducting airways.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: As airways branch toward the periphery, the epithelium gradually transitions to:
o: Simple cuboidal, then simple squamous in alveolar regions
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Epithelial height decreases progressively, becoming squamous at the alveolar level for efficient gas exchange.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: The alveolar-capillary (respiratory) membrane is composed of which layers, in sequence?
o: Alveolar epithelium (type I cell), fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: This thin composite membrane minimizes diffusion distance for gas exchange.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Clara cells (club cells), found in the bronchioles, function to:
o: Produce surfactant exclusively like type II pneumocytes
Secrete protective, protein-rich fluid, detoxify inhaled substances, and serve as regional stem cells
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Club cells protect and can regenerate bronchiolar epithelium, and detoxify inhaled substances.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Cartilage in the bronchial wall is generally arranged as:
o: Absent throughout the entire bronchial tree
Irregular plates/islands, becoming absent in bronchioles
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Cartilage becomes discontinuous plates in bronchi and disappears entirely in bronchioles.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Elastic fibers within the lung parenchyma are important for:
o: Providing elastic recoil, aiding passive expiration
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Elastic tissue enables the lung's passive recoil during expiration.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Arterial blood pH is normally maintained within a narrow range of approximately:
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Normal arterial pH is tightly maintained between 7.35 and 7.45.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relates blood pH to the ratio of:
o: Bicarbonate concentration to dissolved CO2 (via pKa)
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: This equation expresses pH as a function of the bicarbonate/dissolved CO2 ratio.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Respiratory acidosis results from:
o: Hypoventilation, causing CO2 retention and decreased pH
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Inadequate ventilation retains CO2, driving pH down (respiratory acidosis).

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Respiratory alkalosis results from:
o: Hyperventilation, causing excess CO2 elimination and increased pH
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Excess ventilation blows off too much CO2, raising pH (respiratory alkalosis).

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Metabolic acidosis is characterized by:
o: Primary decrease in blood bicarbonate (or excess acid), lowering blood pH, with respiratory compensation (hyperventilation)
Primary increase in CO2 as the initiating problem
Primary increase in blood pH due to bicarbonate excess
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: A primary bicarbonate/acid disturbance defines metabolic acidosis, compensated by hyperventilation.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Metabolic alkalosis is characterized by:
o: Primary increase in blood bicarbonate (or loss of acid), raising blood pH, with respiratory compensation (hypoventilation)
Primary decrease in CO2 as the initiating problem
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Excess bicarbonate or acid loss raises pH, compensated by mild hypoventilation.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis involves:
o: Hyperventilation to reduce CO2, helping normalize pH
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Blowing off CO2 via hyperventilation partially offsets the falling pH from metabolic acidosis.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Renal compensation for a chronic respiratory acidosis involves:
o: Retaining bicarbonate and excreting more hydrogen ions, raising blood bicarbonate to help normalize pH
Excreting more sodium exclusively with no acid-base effect
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: The kidneys compensate for chronic hypercapnia over days by increasing bicarbonate retention.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Common causes of respiratory acidosis include:
o: COPD, opioid overdose, or severe neuromuscular disease impairing ventilation
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Conditions impairing ventilation lead to CO2 retention and respiratory acidosis.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Common causes of respiratory alkalosis include:
o: Anxiety, pain, high altitude, or mechanical overventilation
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Conditions driving excess ventilation cause CO2 washout and respiratory alkalosis.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Pneumonia is characterized histopathologically by:
o: Destruction of alveolar walls with airspace enlargement
Fibrous scarring of the interstitium primarily
Inflammatory exudate filling the alveolar spaces, impairing gas exchange
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Infection fills alveoli with inflammatory exudate, consolidating lung tissue and impairing gas exchange.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Emphysema is characterized by:
o: Destruction of alveolar walls, leading to enlarged airspaces and loss of elastic recoil
Excess mucus production with normal alveolar architecture
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Alveolar wall breakdown enlarges airspaces and reduces elastic recoil, typical of emphysema.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Chronic bronchitis, part of the COPD spectrum, is defined clinically by:
o: Alveolar destruction as the primary feature
A chronic productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years, with airway inflammation and mucus hypersecretion
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: This clinical definition centers on chronic cough/sputum from airway inflammation, not primarily alveolar destruction.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Asthma is characterized by:
o: Reversible airway obstruction due to bronchospasm, inflammation, and mucus hypersecretion
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Asthma's hallmark is reversible airway narrowing driven by inflammation and bronchospasm.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Pulmonary fibrosis is characterized histologically by:
o: Excess deposition of fibrous connective tissue in the interstitium, thickening the alveolar-capillary membrane
Normal alveolar architecture with excess mucus
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Fibrotic scarring thickens the interstitium, impairing diffusion and reducing compliance.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Pulmonary edema, fluid accumulation in the alveoli/interstitium, commonly results from:
o: Increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure (e.g., left heart failure) or increased capillary permeability
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Elevated capillary pressure (cardiogenic) or leaky capillaries (as in ARDS) drive fluid into alveoli/interstitium.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Atelectasis refers to:
o: Collapse of lung tissue/alveoli, reducing gas exchange surface
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Atelectasis is alveolar collapse, reducing the area available for gas exchange.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: A pulmonary embolism most commonly originates from a thrombus in the:
o: Deep veins of the lower limb (deep vein thrombosis)
Pulmonary artery itself, forming de novo
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Most pulmonary emboli arise from dislodged deep venous thrombi in the legs.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: A large pulmonary embolism can cause acute right heart strain because it:
o: Acutely increases pulmonary vascular resistance, increasing the afterload on the right ventricle
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Sudden vascular obstruction raises pulmonary artery pressure, overloading the right ventricle.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Hypoxemia refers to:
o: Decreased partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Hypoxemia specifically denotes low arterial PO2.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Hypoxia refers more broadly to:
o: Inadequate oxygen delivery to or utilization by tissues, which can result from various causes beyond just low PaO2
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Hypoxia is the broader concept of inadequate tissue oxygenation, which hypoxemia is just one cause of.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Hypercapnia refers to:
o: Increased arterial CO2 (PaCO2), usually from hypoventilation
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Hypercapnia is elevated arterial CO2, most often from inadequate alveolar ventilation.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Clubbing of the fingers, seen in some chronic respiratory diseases, is thought to be related to:
o: Chronic hypoxia and other factors affecting peripheral tissue growth signaling
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Clubbing is associated with chronic hypoxic/inflammatory conditions affecting distal digit tissue.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Cystic fibrosis, affecting the CFTR chloride channel, leads to respiratory complications primarily due to:
o: Excessively thin, watery secretions improving clearance
Thick, viscous mucus secretions that impair mucociliary clearance and predispose to chronic infection
Alveolar destruction as the primary initial defect
Pulmonary hypertension as the initial defect
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Defective chloride transport thickens secretions, impairing clearance and promoting infection.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is characterized by:
o: Diffuse alveolar damage and increased capillary permeability, causing severe hypoxemia and pulmonary edema
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: ARDS features widespread alveolar-capillary injury with leaky, edematous, poorly compliant lungs.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Surfactant deficiency contributes to which of the following conditions?
o: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and, to some extent, ARDS
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Insufficient or dysfunctional surfactant contributes to alveolar collapse in these conditions.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Anion gap is used clinically to help classify the cause of:
o: Metabolic acidosis (high anion gap versus normal anion gap causes)
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: The anion gap distinguishes metabolic acidosis subtypes by unmeasured anion accumulation.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis can result from conditions such as:
o: Diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or renal failure (accumulation of unmeasured acids)
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Unmeasured acids like ketones or lactate widen the anion gap in these conditions.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: A normal anion gap metabolic acidosis is classically caused by:
o: Diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis (bicarbonate loss replaced by chloride)
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Bicarbonate loss compensated by chloride retention keeps the anion gap normal (hyperchloremic acidosis).

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Aspirin (salicylate) overdose classically causes a mixed acid-base disturbance featuring:
o: Early respiratory alkalosis (direct respiratory center stimulation) followed by a metabolic acidosis
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory center, then produce a superimposed metabolic acidosis.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Pleural effusion refers to:
o: Collapse of the entire lung always
Abnormal fluid accumulation in the pleural space
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Pleural effusion is excess fluid accumulation within the pleural cavity.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: A transudative pleural effusion, as opposed to exudative, typically results from:
o: Systemic factors altering hydrostatic/oncotic pressure (e.g., heart failure, hypoalbuminemia)
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Transudates arise from systemic pressure/protein imbalances rather than local pleural pathology.

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Silicosis and asbestosis are examples of:
o: Occupational pneumoconioses causing pulmonary fibrosis from inhaled particles
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: These are classic occupational dust-induced fibrotic lung diseases (pneumoconioses).

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.s: Overall respiratory failure is broadly classified into type I (hypoxemic) and type II, which is characterized by:
o: Hypoxemia with hypercapnia, typically from ventilatory failure (e.g., hypoventilation)
Isolated hypercapnia with normal oxygen always
respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.e: Type II respiratory failure combines hypoxemia with hypercapnia, reflecting inadequate ventilation.
